entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:1 "These are the words"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:1 "These are the words" This is the Hebrew title for the book. The Hebrew VERB "spoke" (BDB 180, KB 210, Piel PERFECT) is a COGNATE to the NOUN "words" (BDB 182). Because the book itself says that these are the words of Moses, I believe that this excludes the possibility that this is entirely the work of a later redactor, editor, or compiler. We actually have the words of Moses, which in reality are the words of YHWH (e.g. Deut. 7:4; 11:13-14; 17:3; 29:6). This is not to say that there are not some editorial additions or that Moses recorded his own death. But the bulk of the material and the theology are Mosaic.

Similar phrases seem to divide Deuteronomy into sections:

  1. "These are the words," Deut. 1:1 (1:1-5, introduction to first sermon)
  2. "This is the law," Deut. 4:44 (4:44-49, introduction to second sermon)
  3. "This is the commandment," Deut. 6:1
  4. "These are the words of the covenant," Deut. 29:1 (start of third sermon)
  5. "This is the blessing," Deut. 33:1

While I am commenting on this controversial issue of authorship/date, let me state clearly that I believe all Scripture is inspired (cf. 2 Tim. 3:15-17). The issue of authorship and date are hermeneutical issues, not inspiration issues! The Holy Spirit is the divine author of all canonical texts. Is this pre-suppositional? Absolutely! But it is a crucial presupposition, which must be reviewed and studied before any exegesis of Scripture has validity. The doctrines of Inspiration and Canonization are the twin pillars on which an authoritative Bible rests!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSES' AUTHORSHIP OF THE PENTATEUCH, II

SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH SOURCE CRITICISM (J.E.P.D.)

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "which Moses spoke" There were a large number of people who left Egypt with Moses and it would have been physically impossible for him to speak to all of them at one time. Possibly he spoke to the elders and then they repeated it to smaller groups or this is a literary way of denoting a written document.

▣ "to all Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "across the Jordan" This possibly means "in the region of" (BDB 719). The next two sentences are very specific as to the geographical location of the camp of Israel when Moses gave them this revelation. It became an idiom for

  1. the area east of the Jordan (cf. Num. 35:14; Deut. 1:1,5; 4:41,46,47,49)
  2. the western area (cf. Deut. 3:20,25; 11:30; 9:1)

It requires additional phrases to clarify which bank of the river is meant (cf. R. K Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, pp. 636-638).

▣ "the wilderness" This is not desert but uninhabited pasture land (BDB 184), where the grass is dry and dead most of the year except in winter and early spring.

▣ "the Arabah" This is literally "arid plains" (BDB 787). This refers to the Jordan Valley (i.e. the Great Rift Valley) which goes from the Sea of Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba (really from Turkey to Mozambique). So, it refers to the area both to the south (modern usage) and to the north of the Dead Sea and we are not certain exactly which part is meant. It can refer to the east bank of the Jordan (cf. Deut. 3:17; 4:49) or the west bank (cf. Deut. 11:30). Verse 1 is a summary of the Israelites' trek from Egypt to Sinai.

▣ "Suph" This (Egyptian loan word) is literally "reeds" (BDB 693). This can refer either to salt water plants (cf. 1 Kgs. 9:26; Jon. 2:5) or more commonly fresh water plants (cf. Exod. 2:5). Here it can be translated "area of reeds" or the city of Suph and may relate to Deut. 1:40 (literally, "yom suph, "sea of reeds"), which was translated "Red Sea" by the LXX

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE RED SEA

▣ "Paran" The term "paran" (BDB 803) can refer to a wilderness area which was north of the wilderness of Sinai, but south of the wilderness of Judea (cf. Num. 13:3,26). The oasis of Kadesh-Barnea was located in this wilderness area.

However, in this verse Paran seems to be an unknown location (possibly a city) on the eastern bank of the Jordan.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WILDERNESSES OF THE EXODUS

▣ "Topel" The term means "whitewash" (BDB 1074). This is an unknown site, but is apparently on the eastern side of the Jordan in the territory of Moab.

▣ "Laban" This is one of several campsites of Israel in Sinai. The term means "white" (BDB 526 III). This is an unknown site. Some scholars place it on the route from Sinai to Moab (cf. Libnah of Num. 33:20-21), while others make it a city or village on the eastern bank of the Jordan in Moab.

▣ "Hazeroth" It is this place name (BDB 348) that has caused scholars to assert that the locations mentioned after "Arabah" are Israel's camp locations between Mt. Sinai and the plains of Moab (cf. Deut. 1:2). If so, Laban would be Libnah (cf. Num. 33:20-21) and Hazeroth would refer to Num. 33:17-18. This was the site where Aaron and Miriam murmured against Moses' leadership or his new marriage to a Cushite woman (cf. Numbers 12).

▣ "Dizahab" This name (BDB 191) is a combination of Aramaic "place of" and Hebrew "gold." The rabbis related this to the Egyptians giving the Israelites gold when they left Egypt (cf. Exod. 3:22; 11:2; 12:35), but in context, this was a place name. The site is unknown. It was either

  1. on the east bank of the Jordan in Moab and thereby close to the other places mentioned
  2. on the route from Mt. Sinai to Moab

entries.title: Deuteronomy Introduction
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
INTRODUCTION TO DEUTERONOMY

  1. SIGNIFICANCE

    1. It is one of the four OT books quoted most often in the NT (i.e. Genesis, Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Isaiah). Deuteronomy is quoted 83 times.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH

    2. A quote from the Tyndale OT Commentary Series, "Deuteronomy," by J. A. Thompson:
       "Deuteronomy is one of the greatest books of the Old Testament. Its influence on the domestic and personal religion of all ages has not been surpassed by any other book in the Bible" (p. 11).

    3. This must have been one of Jesus' favorite books of the OT:
      1. He quoted repeatedly from it during His temptation by Satan in the wilderness
        1. Matt. 4:4; Luke 4:4 ‒ Deut. 8:3
        2. Matt. 4:7; Luke 4:12 ‒ Deut. 6:26
        3. Matt. 4:10; Luke 4:8 ‒ Deut. 6:13
      2. It is possibly the outline behind the Sermon on the Mount (cf. Matthew 5-7).
      3. Jesus quoted Deut. 6:5 as the greatest commandment (cf. Matt. 22:34-40; Mark 12:28-34; Luke 10:25-28).
      4. Jesus quoted this section of the OT (i.e. Torah, Genesis‒Deuteronomy) most often because the Jews of His day considered it the most authoritative section of the canon.

    4. This is one major example in the Scripture of the reinterpretation of a previous revelation by God to a new situation. An example of this would be the slight difference between the Ten Commandments in Exod. 20:11 versus Deut. 5:15. Exodus 20 was given at Mt. Sinai and relates to the Wilderness Wandering Period, while Deuteronomy 5 was given on the Plains of Moab preparing the people for a settled life in Canaan.

    5. Deuteronomy is a series of messages given by Moses on the Plains of Moab (eastern Jordan). The three sermons all begin with the designation of the physical place of the sermon. All may refer to the same place.
      1. "across the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel and Laban and Hazeroth and Dizahab," Deut. 1:1
      2. "across the Jordan in the land of Moab," Deut. 1:5
      3. "across the Jordan, in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon the king," Deut. 4:46
      4. "in the land of Moab," Deut. 29:1
        SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSES' AUTHORSHIP OF THE PENTATEUCH

    6. Deuteronomy is also the center of dialogue today among OT scholars concerning its literary formation. Modern scholarship is divided on its theories regarding the compositions of both Deuteronomy and rest of the Pentateuch.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH SOURCE CRITICISM, I. C.

  2. THE NAME OF THE BOOK

    1. In Hebrew the titles of the books of the Tanakh (Pentateuch) are one of their first ten words, usually their first word:
      1. Genesis, "In the beginning"
      2. Exodus, "And these are the names"
      3. Leviticus, "And He called"
      4. Numbers, "In the desert"
      5. Deuteronomy, "And these are the words"

    2. In the Talmud Deuteronomy is called "repetition of the law" (Mishnah Hattorah from Deut.17:18).

    3. In the Greek translation of the OT, called the Septuagint (LXX), written around 250 B.C., Deuteronomy is called "the second law" because of a mistranslation of Deut. 17:18 (i.e. "make a copy of this law").
      SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

    4. We get our English title from Jerome's Latin Vulgate which calls it "the second law" (Deuteronomium).

    5. It is a book of instructions on how to keep God's covenant.
      1. "this book of the law," Deut. 28:61
      2. "this law," Deut. 1:5; 4:8; 17:18,19; 27:3,8,26
      3. other descriptive phrases, Deut. 4:1,45; 6:17, 20; 12:1

  3. CANONIZATION ‒ This is the concluding book of The Torah which forms the first of the three divisions of the Hebrew canon

    1. The Torah or Law — Genesis ‒ Deuteronomy

    2. The Prophets:
      1. Former Prophets — Joshua ‒ Kings (except Ruth)
      2. Latter Prophets — Isaiah ‒ Malachi (except Daniel and Lamentations)

    3. The Writings:
      1. The Megilloth (5 scrolls):
        1. Song of Songs
        2. Ecclesiastes
        3. Ruth
        4. Lamentations
        5. Esther
      2. Daniel
      3. Wisdom Literature:
        1. Job
        2. Psalms
        3. Proverbs
      4. 1 and 2 Chronicles

        SPECIAL TOPIC: CANON (Hebrew)

  4. GENRE

    1. Deuteronomy is a mixture of several genres.
      1. historical narrative (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HISTORICAL NARRATIVE)
        1. Deuteronomy 1-4
        2. Deuteronomy 34
      2. exhortations ‒ Deuteronomy 6-11
      3. guidelines, Deut. 12-28
      4. psalms/hymns/songs ‒ Deuteronomy 32
      5. blessings ‒ Deuteronomy 33

        "Bible Interpretation Seminar"

    2. Deuteronomy describes itself as a book of guidelines from YHWH for life (Torah) in Deut. 29:21; 30:10; 31:26. It is a book of teachings about faith and life to be passed on to future generations. See full note at Deut. 4:9.

    3. God's special leader is replaced by God's written revelation. Human leaders will come and go, but the written revelation is emphasized as authoritative.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

  5. AUTHORSHIP

    1. Jewish Tradition:
      1. Ancient tradition is unanimous that the author was Moses.
      2. This is stated in:
        1. Talmud ‒ Baba Bathra 14b
        2. Mishnah
        3. Ben Sirach's Ecclesiasticus 24:23 (written about 185 B.C.)
        4. Philo of Alexandria
        5. Flavius Josephus
      3. The Scripture itself:
        1. Judges 3:4 and Joshua 8:31
        2. "Moses spoke":
          (1) Deut. 1:1, 3
          (2) Deut. 5:1
          (3) Deut. 27:1
          (4) Deut. 29:2
          (5) Deut. 31:1, 30
          (6) Deut. 32:44
          (7) Deut. 33:1
        3. "YHWH spoke to Moses"
          (1) Deut. 5:4-5, 22
          (2) Deut. 6:1
          (3) Deut. 10:1
        4. "Moses wrote":
          (1) Deut. 31:9, 22, 24
          (2) Exodus 17:14
          (3) Exodus 24:4, 12
          (4) Exodus 34:27-28
          (5) Numbers 33:2
        5. Jesus quotes from or alludes to Deuteronomy and states "Moses said"/"Moses wrote":
          (1) Matt. 19:7-9; Mark 10:4-5 ‒ Deut. 24:1-4
          (2) Mark 7:10 ‒ Deut. 5:16
          (3) Luke 16:31; 24:27, 44; John 5:46-47; 7:19, 23
        6. Paul asserts Moses as author:
          (1) Rom. 10:19 ‒ Deut. 32:21
          (2) 1 Cor. 9:9 ‒ Deut. 25:4
          (3) Gal. 3:10 ‒ Deut. 27:26
          (4) Acts 26:22; 28:23
        7. Peter asserts Moses as author in his Pentecostal sermon ‒ Acts 3:22
        8. The author of Hebrews asserts Moses as author ‒ Heb. 10:28; Deut. 17:2-6

    2. Modern Scholarship
      1. Many of the 18th and 19th century theologians, following the Graf-Wellhausen theory of multiple authorship (JEDP), assert that Deuteronomy was written by a priest/prophet during Josiah's reign in Judah to support his spiritual reform. This would mean that the book was written in Moses' name about 621 B.C.
      2. They base this on:
        1. 2 Kgs. 22:8; 2 Chr. 34:14-15, "I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord"
        2. Deuteronomy 2 discussed a single site for the tabernacle and later temple
        3. Deuteronomy 17 discussed a later king
        4. the truth that writing a book in the name of a famous person from the past was common in the ancient Near East and in Jewish circles
        5. similarities of style, vocabulary and grammar between Deuteronomy and Joshua, Kings and Jeremiah
        6. Deuteronomy records the death of Moses (Deuteronomy 34)
        7. obvious later editorial additions in the Pentateuch:
           (1) Deut. 3:14
           (2) Deut. 34:6
        8. the sometimes unexplainable variety in the use of the names of Deity: El, El Shaddai, Elohim, YHWH, in seemingly unified contexts and historical periods.
          SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PENTATEUCH

    3. There are obviously some editorial additions. Jewish scribes were trained in Egypt where they regularly updated ancient texts. Mesopotamian scribes were reluctant to add material.
       Some examples in Deuteronomy are:
      1. Deut. 27:3,8
      2. Deut. 28:58
      3. Deut. 29:21,29
      4. Deut. 30:10,19
      5. Deut. 31:24

        SPECIAL TOPIC: LATER EDITORIAL ADDITIONS TO THE PENTATEUCH, II.

  6. DATE

    1. If written by Moses there are still two possibilities related to the time and duration of the Exodus from Egypt:
      1. If 1 Kgs. 6:1 is meant to be taken literally then about 1445 B.C. (18th dynasty of Thutmose III and Amenhotep II):
        1. LXX has 440 years instead of 480 years
        2. This number may reflect generations not years (symbolic)
      2. Archaeological evidences for 1290 B.C. for the Exodus (19th Egyptian dynasty):
        1. Seti I (1390-1290) moved Egyptian capital from Thebes to delta region ‒ Zoan/Tanis.
        2. Rameses II (1290-1224):
          (1) His name occurs in a city built by Hebrew slaves (cf. Gen. 47:11; Exod.1:11)
          (2) He had 47 daughters
          (3) He was not succeeded by his oldest son
        3. All major walled cities of Palestine destroyed and rapidly rebuilt about 1250 B.C.

          SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DATE OF THE EXODUS

    2. Modern Scholarship theory of multiple authorship:
      1. J (YHWH) 950 B.C. (written in southern Israel)
      2. E (Elohim) 850 B.C. (written in northern Israel)
      3. JE (combination) 750 B.C.
      4. D (Deuteronomy) 621 B.C. (a copy of the Law found in the temple)
      5. P (Priests) 400 B.C. (final edit related to rituals and procedures)

        SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH SOURCE CRITICISM

  7. SOURCES FOR CORROBORATING THE HISTORICAL SETTING

    1. The Hittite treaties of the 2nd millennium B.C. offer us an ancient, historically contemporary parallel to the structure of Deuteronomy (as well as Exodus-Leviticus and Joshua 24). This treaty pattern changed by the 1st millennium B.C. This gives us evidence for the historicity of Deuteronomy. For further reading in this area, see G. E. Mendenhall's Law and Covenants in Israel and The Ancient Near East and M. G. Kline, Treaty of the Great King; K. A. Kitchen, Ancient Orient and the OT, pp. 92-102; and D. Brent Sandy and Ronald L. Giese, Cracking OT Codes, pp. 125-128.

    2. The Hittite pattern and its Deuteronomy parallels:
      1. Preamble (Deut. 1:1-5, introduction of speaker, YHWH)
      2. Review of the past acts of the King (Deut. 1:6-4:49, God's past acts for Israel)
      3. Treaty terms (Deut. 5-26):
        1. General (Deut. 5-11)
        2. Specific (Deut. 12-26)
      4. Results of treaty (Deut. 27-29):
        1. Benefits (Deut. 28)
        2. Consequences (Deut. 27)
      5. Witness of deity (Deut. 30:19; 31:19, also 32, Moses' song functions as a witness):
        1. a copy of the Treaty placed in temple of the deity
        2. a copy of the Treaty kept in the temple of the vassal to be read annually
        3. the uniqueness of the Hittite treaties from the later Assyrian and Syrian treaties were:
          (1) the historical review of the past acts of the king
          (2) the cursing section was less pronounced

    3. The Hittite treaty pattern was slightly changed (one item dropped) in the first millennium B.C. The form of Deuteronomy fits the time of Moses and Joshua best!

    4. For a good discussion of these Hittite treaties see K. A. Kitchen, Ancient Orient and Old Testament, pp. 99-102.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: HITTITE (Suzerain) TREATIES

  8. LITERARY UNITS (context)

    1. Introduction to the book, Deut. 1:1-5

    2. First Sermon, Deut. 1:6-4:43 (The past acts of YHWH for today)

    3. Second Sermon, Deut. 4:44-26:19 (The law of YHWH for today and for all days)
      1. General ‒ the Ten Commandments (Deuteronomy 5-11)
      2. Specific examples and applications (Deuteronomy 12-26)

    4. Third Sermon, Deut. 27-30 (YHWH's Law for the future Deuteronomy 27-29)
      1. Cursings (Deuteronomy 27)
      2. Blessings (Deuteronomy 28)
      3. Covenant renewal (Deuteronomy 29-30)

    5. Last Words of Moses, Deut. 31-33
      1. "Good bye" sermon, Deut. 31:1-29
      2. The song of Moses, Deut. 31:30-32:52
      3. The blessings of Moses Deut. 33:1-29

    6. Moses' death, Deuteronomy 34

  9. MAIN TRUTHS

    1. Final preparations before entering the Promised Land. God's Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15) has been fulfilled!
      SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

    2. Genesis 12:1-3 promised a land and a seed. The OT focuses on the land; the NT will focus on "the seed" (cf. Galatians 3).

    3. Moses prepares the people for a settled agricultural life versus a nomadic life. He adapts the Sinai Covenant for the Promised Land. In a sense Deuteronomy is Israel's constitution.

    4. The book emphasizes God's faithfulness in the past, the present, and the future. The covenant, however, is conditional (i.e. Deuteronomy 30)! Israel must respond and continue in faith, repentance and obedience. If she does not the curses of Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29 will become a reality. Moses is a prime example of God's love and justice! Even God's special leader is responsible for obedience. Disobedience always carries consequences!
      SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT
      SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley

* Although they are not inspired, paragraph divisions are the key to understanding and following the original author's intent. Each modern translation has divided and summarized the paragraphs. Every paragraph has one central topic, truth, or thought. Each version encapsulates that topic in its own distinct way. As you read the text, ask yourself which translation fits your understanding of the subject and verse divisions.

In every chapter we must read the Bible first and try to identify its subjects (paragraphs), then compare our understanding with the modern versions. Only when we understand the original author's intent by following his logic and presentation can we truly understand the Bible. Only the original author is inspired—readers have no right to change or modify the message. Bible readers do have the responsibility of applying the inspired truth to their day and their lives.

Note that all technical terms and abbreviations are explained fully in the following Special Topics: Hebrew Grammatical Tems, Textual Criticism, and Glossary.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:2 "eleven days journey from Horeb. . .Kadesh-barnea"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:2 "eleven days journey from Horeb. . .Kadesh-barnea" This verse may be a summary of the movement of Israel from Mt. Horeb/Sinai to the oasis at Kadesh, but if so, it does not fit well between Deut. 1:1 and 3. This may have been included to show that the journey should have taken eleven days, but because of unbelief (cf. Num. 13-14) it took a whole generation (38 years plus). This eleven-day trip seems to confirm the site of Mt. Horeb/Sinai as in the southern tip of the Sinai Peninsula.

Notice that the place of the giving of the law is called "Horeb." Horeb is a Hebrew word for "waste" or "desolate" (BDB 352, KB 349). Sinai (BDB 696) is a non-Hebrew word. The two terms are used synonymously. However, it is possible that "Horeb" refers to a mountain range in the southern Sinai peninsula and "Sinai" refers to the highest peak. They refer to the place where Moses brought Israel to meet YHWH (e.g. Horeb, Exod. 3:1; Deut. 1:6,19; 4:10,15; 5:12 and Sinai Exod. 19; Lev. 7:38; 25:1; 26:46; 27:34; Num. 1:1,9; 3:1,4,14; 9:1,5).

Why the name "Horeb" is used most often in Deuteronomy (except Deut. 33:2) and "Sinai" most often in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers is unknown. There is literary variety in the writings of Moses. This could refer to:

  1. Moses using different scribes
  2. changes by later scribes for unknown reasons
  3. literary variety
  4. normal variations involving oral traditions (see Walton, D. Brent Sandy, The Lost World of Scripture)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE EXODUS (The Route, III.)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE LOCATION OF MT. SINAI

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOREB

▣ "Mount Seir" BDB 973 says the term "Seir" can mean

  1. goat
  2. hairy
  3. hairy as in well-wooded with trees
  4. KB 1989 asserts that it means "hairy"

In the OT this term is associated with the mountainous region of Edom (cf. Gen. 14:6; 36:20-21,30; Deut. 1:2,44; 2:1,4-5; 33:2). It is often characterized as a mountain (cf. Gen. 14:6; 36:8-9; Deut. 2:1). Therefore, originally it was a Horite mountainous area annexed by Edom.

▣ "Kadesh-barnea" This is a large oasis on the border of Edom (cf. Num. 20:16), about 50 miles south of Beersheba, with four natural springs.

Its name has two elements. The first is from the Hebrew for "holy" (BDB 873). The second is unknown. It became the hub of their wilderness wanderings (cf. Numbers 13-14) for 38 yeras until the unbelieving generation died. Both Miriam and Aaron died here (cf. Num: 20:1,2b).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:3 "the fortieth year"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:3 "the fortieth year" This is the only date in Deuteronomy. "Forty" (BDB 917) is used so often in the Bible that it seems to refer to a long, indefinite period of time. The actual chronology seems to be 38 years (from Sinai to the plains of Moab).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

SPECIAL TOPIC: DATE OF THE EXODUS

▣ "on the first day of the eleventh month" The author is making every effort to locate the place and time of these words to Israel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANCIENT NEAR EASTERN CALENDARS

▣ "Moses spoke to the children of Israel, according to all that the Lord had commanded him to give to them" YHWH is the author; Moses is the channel, but all these commands come from the covenant-making God.

There is great variety in the names for Deity in Moses' writings. The following is an example from Deuteronomy 1-4.

  1. The Lord (YHWH), Deut. 1:3,8,27,34,37,41,42,43,45; 2:12,14,15,17,21,31; 3:2,20,21,26 (twice); 4:12,14,15,21,27
  2. The Lord (YHWH) our God (Elohim), Deut. 1:1,19,20,25,41; 2:29,36,37; 3:3; 4:7
  3. The Lord (YHWH) your God (Elohim), Deut. 1:10,21,26,30,31,32; 2:7(twice),30; 3:18,20,21,22; 4:2,3,4,10,19,21,23 (twice),24,25,29,30,31,34,40
  4. The Lord (YHWH), the God (Elohim) of your fathers, Deut. 1:11,21; 4:1
  5. God (Elohim), Deut. 1:17; 2:33; 4:24 (jealous God), 31(compassionate God), 32,33
  6. Lord (Adon) God (YHWH), Deut. 3:24
  7. Lord (YHWH), my God (Elohim), Deut. 4:5
  8. Lord (YHWH), He is God (Elohim), Deut. 4:35,39

There has been much speculation about this variety:

  1. multiple authors
  2. multiple scribes
  3. theological distinctives
  4. literary variety

OT scholars must admit that the authorship, compilation, editing, and scribal activity connected to the Canonical books of the OT is a mystery. We must be careful to not let our modern western literary theories or our a-priori theological assumptions demand one and only one interpretation. Mystery means mystery.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C. and D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSES' AUTHORSHIP OF THE PENTATEUCH

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PENTATEUCH, II.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH SOURCE CRITICISM (J.E.P.D.)

1:4
NASB NRSV, JPSOA  "after he defeated"
NKJV, Peshitta  "after he had killed"
TEV  "after the Lord had defeated"
NJB  "He had defeated"
LXX  "after he had struck"

The VERB (BDB 645, KB 697, Hiphil INFINITIVE) means "to smite" with the grammatical and theological implication is that it was YHWH. He is the first cause and only cause (i.e. Isa. 14:24-27; 45:7; Amos 3:6)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

▣ "Sihon" Sihon (BDB 695) was the Amorite king of a region next to Og, king of Bashan, on the eastern side of Jordan. Moses was commanded by God (cf. Deut. 2:4-9) not to attack the Israelites' relatives of Moab and Edom (Lot's descendants by his own daughters, cf. Gen. 19:30-38). The only other route to the Jordan was through Sihon's kingdom. The capital city of Heshbon was the first major city that the Israeli army conquered (cf. Deut. 2:26-37; Num. 21:21-32).

▣ "Og" Og (BDB 728) was the Amorite king of this region called Bashan, which had two large cities (cf. Josh. 12:4) and many villages (cf. Deut. 3:1-10). He was apparently one of the Rephaim (giants, cf. Deut. 3:11) who inhabited Canaan (cf. Deut. 2:20; Josh 12:4). It was the descendants of these giants (cf. Deut. 2:11) at Hebron who had caused Israel to reject the two faithful spies' report (cf. Num. 13:22).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DATE OF THE EXODUS

SPECIAL TOPIC: PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE

▣ "Astaroth" This city (BDB 800) was named after the female consort of the Canaanite fertility god Baal. She was called Asherah or Astarte in Canaan. Because of the mentioning of Rephaim, it is possible that this city is referenced in Gen. 14:5.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "Edrei" This was one of the capital cities of Og (BDB 204, cf. Josh. 12:4; 13:12).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:5 "in the land of Moab"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:5 "in the land of Moab" This is where the Israelites camped before entering the Promised Land. It is the location just north of the Dead Sea on the eastern bank of the Jordan, where Deuteronomy was written.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOAB

▣ "Moses undertook" This VERB (BDB 383, KB 381, Hiphil PERFECT) implies "volitional commitment" (cf. Gen. 18:27; Exod. 2:21; Jdg. 19:6).

▣ "to expound this law" This VERB (BDB 91, KB 106, Piel PERFECT) means to "make clear" or "understandable." This word only appears here and two other times where it is translated "write" (cf. Deut. 27:8; Hab. 2:2). Instruction which is not clear or understandable is useless and, in this covenantal context, dangerous.

The term "law" (i.e. torah, BDB 435) is the Hebrew term for "teaching" or "instruction" (cf. Deut. 4:8,44; 27:3,8,26; 28:58,61; 29:20,28; 30:10; 31:9,11,12; 32:46). In this context it refers to Moses' sermons delivered to Israel on the eastern side of Jordan across from Jericho, on the plains of Moab, just before the Israelites crossed the Jordan without him.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR GOD'S REVELATION, II. B.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAWS IN THE ANE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:6 "Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:6 "Lord" This is the unique name for the covenant God of Israel (i.e. YHWH, BDB 217, cf. Gen. 2:4). It is used of God as Savior, Redeemer, and covenant-making God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "our God" The personal PLURAL PRONOUN implies a covenant relationship, initiated and accepted at Sinai. This is the name of Deity, "Elohim" (BDB 43). It is used of God as Creator, Provider, and Sustainer of all creation (e.g. Gen. 1:1-2:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY C.

▣ "Horeb" See note at Deut. 1:2 and SPECIAL TOPIC: LOCATION OF MT. SINAI.

▣ "'You have stayed long enough at this mountain'" YHWH now tells the people it is time for them to do what He initially had commanded them, occupy Canaan (cf. Gen. 15:13-21; Numbers 13-14)! They had stayed at Mt. Horeb for about one year (compare Exod. 19:1 with Num. 10:11).

1:7
NASB  "Turn and set your journey"
NKJV  "Turn and take your journey"
NRSV  "Resume your journey"
TEV  "Break camp and move on"
JPSOA  "Start out and make your way"
LXX  "turn, and depart"

The first VERB (BDB 815, KB 937, Qal IMPERATIVE) means "turn," but is used in several senses:

  1. turn to look at something/someone, Exod. 2:12; 16:10; Num. 12:10
  2. turn so as to change direction, Gen. 18:22; 24:49; Exod. 14:25; 21:33; Deut. 1:7,24; 2:3; 9:15; 10:5
  3. turn to other gods, Lev. 19:4; Deut. 29:18; 30:17; 31:18,20
  4. seek help from, Lev. 19:31; 20:6
  5. the approach of
    1. evening, Deut. 23:11
    2. morning, Exod. 14:27

The second VERB (BDB 652, KB 704, Qal IMPERATIVE) means "pull out," "pull up," or "set out," which is used often in Numbers for the Israelites moving their camp site. This usage continues in Deuteronomy (e.g. 1:7,19,40; 2:1,24). It originally referred to pulling up the tent stakes.

▣ "and go" This is the third parallel Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 97, KB 112).

▣ There are five topological divisions of Palestine running north to south mentioned:

  1. "in the hill country of the Amorite" ‒ This refers to the eastern bank of the Jordan and the kingdoms of Sihon and Og.
  2. "in the Arabah" ‒ This refers to the Jordan rift valley south of the Dead Sea (BDB 787, cf. Deut. 1:1,7; 2:8; 3:17; 4:49; 11:30; Josh. 8:14; 11:2,16; 12:3; 18:18)
  3. "in the hill country and in the lowlands" ‒ This refers to the area west and south of the Dead Sea, later to become the tribal allocation of Ephraim and Judah.
  4. "the Negev" ‒ This is the arid desert land south of the Dead Sea and to the west (BDB 616)
  5. "by the seacoast" ‒ This is the coastal plain running from Egypt to Lebanon (i.e. Shephelah, BDB 410)

All of these taken together refer to the land promised to Abraham in Genesis 15.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GEOGRAPHICAL DIVISIONS OF THE PROMISED LAND

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:8 Verse 8 is a series of commands:

  1. "See" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "Go in" ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "Possess" ‒ BDB 439, KB 441, Qal IMPERATIVE

▣ "'I have placed the land before you'" The Hebrew term for "have placed" is the same as "given" (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT). YHWH was now giving them the land as He had promised Abraham (Gen. 12:1, line 5; 15:12-21; Exod. 6:8), but they had to possess it. Notice the conditional aspect of even this foundational covenant (e.g. Deut. 4:1; 5:33; 6:18; 8:1; 16:20; 30:16,19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "possess the land" See SPECIAL TOPIC: POSSESS THE LAND

▣ "the land which the Lord swore to give to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob" See Deut. 4:37; 6:10; 9:5; 10:11,15; 30:20; Gen. 12:5-7; 13:14-17; 15:18; 26:3; Exod. 32:13; 33:1. This land would include the area from Kadesh-Barnea in the south to Byblos and Zephan, Zedad and Lebo-hamath in the north (possibly even as far east as the head waters of the Euphrates, cf. Gen. 15:18). See MacMillan Bible Atlas, p. 47.

There are several places where the general boundaries of the Promised Land are given (Exod. 34:1-12; Deut. 1:6-8; 3:12-20; 11:24; Josh. 1:3-4). It was only during David's and Solomon's reigns that this whole general area was under Israel's control.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:9 "at that time"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:9 "at that time" This is a recurrent phrase in Deuteronomy. The first four chapters are a review of YHWH's gracious acts on Israel's behalf. This idiom is a way of denoting a past act (cf. Deut. 1:9,16,18; 2:34; 3:4,8,12,18;4:14).

▣ "I am not able to bear the burden of you alone" There are two possibel references.

  1. Exodus 18:13-26 for Jethro's advice to Moses about this very problem (i.e. Moses being the only judge)
  2. Numbers 11:12-14 where Moses uses these very words to describe the problems associated with trying to govern Israel

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:10 "the Lord your God has multiplied you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:10 "the Lord your God has multiplied you" This was part of YHWH's promise to the Patriarchs (e.g. Gen. 13:16; 17:2,20; 22:17; 48:4; Lev. 26:9; Deut. 7:13).

▣ "as the stars of heaven" This phrase is also found in Gen. 15:5; 22:17; 26:4; Exod. 32:13; Deut. 10:22; 28:62. Other parallel phrases used to portray uncountable numbers (cf. Gen. 16:10) of Israelites are: "dust of the earth" (cf. Gen. 12:1; 13:16; 28:14; Num. 23:10); and "sand of the sea" (cf. Gen. 22:17; 32:12). All of these from a man who was childless until age 100 (i.e. Abraham)!

In Deut. 1:28 the Israelites, who are more numerous than the stars, are afraid of the inhabitants of Canaan because of their:

  1. numbers
  2. size
  3. walled cities

What irony!

See full note at Gen. 13:16.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:11 "the God of your fathers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:11 "the God of your fathers" This often repeated designation asserts that the same God who spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is still active in the lives and destiny of their descendants.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "increase you a thousand-fold" This is obviously an idiomatic phrase. The number 1,000 was a multiple of ten (times 3) and, therefore, a symbol of greatness or numerousness (cf. Ps. 90:4; 2 Pet. 3:8). Here is a list of hyperbolic usages from NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 417:

  1. the work of God in blessing, Deut. 1:11; Job 42:12; Ps. 144:13
  2. military blessing, Josh. 23:10
  3. military curse for unbelief, Deut. 32:30; Isa. 7:23; 30:17; Amos 5:3
  4. enduring sovereignty of God, Ps. 90:4
  5. God's covenant promises, Deut. 7:9; Ps. 105:8
  6. God's wrath vs. God's love, Exod. 34:7; Deut. 5:9-10
  7. blessing of being in God's temple, Ps. 84:10

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:12 "strife"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:12 "strife" This means "lawsuit" (BDB 936).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:13 "Choose"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:13 "Choose" This VERB (BDB 396, KB 393) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. Notice that Moses was commanding the people (i.e. their leaders) to take responsibility (they choose) for the community along with himself (Moses appoints). These new judges (i.e. tribal leaders) were to be:

  1. "wise" ‒ (BDB 314) meaning capable of thoughtful and godly choices (e.g. Joseph, Gen. 41:33,39; military leaders, Exod. 18:21; David, 2 Sam. 14:20; Solomon, 1 Kgs. 2:9; 3:12; 5:21)
  2. "discerning" ‒ (BDB 106, KB 122, Niphal PARTICIPLE) meaning someone who has discretion, discernment, and intelligence (e.g. Joseph, Gen. 41:33; negative in Jer. 4:22)
  3. "experience" ‒ (BDB 393, KB 390, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE). This is a common word with a large semantic field.
    1. NASB, TEV, NJB, JPSOA ‒ experienced
    2. NKJB ‒ knowledgeable
    3. NRSV, REB ‒ reputable
    4. JB ‒ tested
    5. NIV ‒ respected
    6. NET ‒ known

SPECIAL TOPIC: HE CHOSE US, I. B.

▣ "I will appoint them" The VERB (BDB 962, KB 1321) is a Qal IMPERFECT, used in the sense of a COHORTATIVE. Moses set or appointed these chosen men to places of leadership and judgment (e.g. Exod. 1:11; 18:21; Deut. 17:14,15; Jdg. 11:11). However, in reality, it was YHWH who "took" (BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERFECT with waw, Deut. 1:15) them, which denotes God's choice (e.g. Deut. 4:20,34; 1 Kgs. 11:37). The human process followed a divine plan!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:15 "leaders of thousands, and of hundreds, of fifties and of tens"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:15 "leaders of thousands, and of hundreds, of fifties and of tens" These divisions later became the names of military units (cf. Exod. 18:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

▣
NASB  "leaders"
NKJV, LXX  "officers"
NRSV, TEV  "officials"
NJB  "scribes"
REB, Peshitta  "commanders"
JPSOA  "heads"

This term (BDB 1009) originally referred to a scribe (i.e. one who organizes), but this does not seem to fit its usage in Deut. 1:15; 20:5,8,9; or Josh. 1:10,32. In this context it seems to refer to a lesser judge or military helper to tribal leaders.

The UBS Handbook for Translators on Deuteronomy says, "they appear with elders (Num. 11:16) and with judges (Deut. 16:18; Josh. 8:33), and also in military contexts (Deut. 20:5,8,9; Josh. 1:10; 3:2)" p. 26.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:16 "alien"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:16 "alien" Non-Jews (lit. "sojourners" or "resident aliens," BDB 158) were to be treated as equals in the legal realm (cf. Lev. 19:33-34,35). Israel was to deal with them graciously (cf. Lev. 23:22; Deut. 10:19; 14:29; 24:14,17,19-21; 27:19). Israel had been aliens in Egypt (cf. Exod. 22:21; 23:9; Deut. 10:18-19) and knew how it felt!

▣ "righteously" See SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:16-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:16-17 Moses charged these new tribal judges to be impartial (cf. Deut. 16:19; 24:17). Impartiality is a characteristic of God (cf. Deut. 10:17). Israel was meant to be a people and society that revealed the character of YHWH so that the world would come to place their trust and faith in Him. Since the Fall (i.e. Genesis 3) this has been God's plan. Israel failed, but the ideal Israelite (i.e. Jesus, cf. Gen. 3:15; Isaiah 53) succeeded (e.g. John 14:5-7, 8-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:17 "You shall not show partiality in judgment"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:17 "You shall not show partiality in judgment" The term "partiality" is literally "face" (BDB 815). The VERB (BDB 647, KB 699, Hiphil IMPERFECT) means "to regard." The point being that as a person approached the judge, the judge should not attempt to see or recognize who it was coming before him, but to hear the case fairly and impartially. The judge was to treat all cases without prejudice (cf. Lev. 19:15).

▣ "You shall not fear man" This VERB (BDB 158 III, KB 185, Qal IMPERFECT) means "dread" or "awe." In this context "dread" is demanded. In Deuteronomy this term is used in two contexts. God's leaders/judges are not to fear the reactions of men to their decisions (Deut. 1:17) and God's people are not to fear the messages of false prophets (Deut. 18:22).

This term is used often in the Psalms to express the covenant believer's respect and awe of YHWH (e.g. Deut. 33:8; 22:23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

▣ "The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me" Moses was YHWH's representative to the people (i.e. "judge"). He was also seen as a prophet (cf. Deut. 1:18; 18:15-22).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:19 "Horeb"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:19 "Horeb" The two titles of the sacred mountains, Horeb and Sinai, are used synonymously. Horeb is a Semitic term. Sinai is not semitic but possibly relates to the Wilderness of Sin. Sin is a term for a small desert plant common in the region. Some believe that Horeb is the mountain range and Sinai is the peak, but we don't really know for certain. See full note at Deut. 1:2.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOREB

▣ "that great and terrible wilderness" Usually the term "wilderness" (BDB 184) means uninhabited pastureland, but this trek took them across the desert of the Sinai Peninsula. There were few sources of natural water. YHWH provided water and food for them supernaturally during this forty year period. Today, this desert is called Et Tih, which means "the wandering." This journey was about 100 miles and crossed very rough country (i.e. Deut. 8:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WILDERNESSES OF THE EXODUS

▣ "the hill country of the Amorites" This would refer to the southern part of the land of Canaan (i.e. Negev, Arabah).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GEOGRAPHICAL DIVISIONS OF THE PROMISED LAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE

▣ "just as the Lord our God had commanded us" For the names for Deity see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C. and D. YHWH led them by

  1. Moses' words
  2. the Shekinah cloud of glory, which rested over the tabernacle. When it moved Israel followed.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CLOUD. . .THE PILLAR

▣ "we came to Kadesh-barnea" The Hebrew word for holy is kadosh (BDB 871), from which we get "Kadesh." Kadesh-barnea means "holy" or "separated," possibly "holy city," "holy place, or "separated place." It was an important campground for the Israelites as it was for Abraham because it was the largest oasis in the area (i.e. about 50 miles south of Beer-sheba) in the wilderness of Paran (LXX of Num. 33:36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:19-25 "Then we set out"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:19-25 "Then we set out" The VERB (BDB 652, KB 704, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) is regularly used of the Exodus (cf. Exod. 12:37; 13:20; 14:15; 16:1; and often in Numbers 33). These verses relate to the journey from Mt. Sinai to Kadesh-barnea.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOCATION OF MT. SINAI

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:20-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:20-21 These verses have caused problems for commentators because of the change in usage between the PRONOUNS "our" and "your," which is common throughout the book of Deuteronomy. This is one reason why some believe that Deuteronomy was written by several people. I think that Moses wrote (or dictated) the majority of the revelations, but it is obvious that his writings have been edited by later scribes and may contain the comments of the original scribe or later scribe.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSAIC AUTHORSHIP OF THE PENTATEUCH

SPECIAL TOPIC: LATER SCRIBAL ADDITIONS, II.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:21 "See, the Lord your God has placed. . .take possession"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:21 "See, the Lord your God has placed. . .take possession" This may be a reference to Deut. 1:8, where YHWH, through Moses, told the people to possess the land which He had promised to the Patriarchs (cf. Deut. 12:5-7; 13:14-17; 15:18; 26:3).

This verse, like Deut. 1:7 and 8, contains several commands:

  1. "See" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "Go up" ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "Take possession" ‒ BDB 439, KB 441, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. "Do not fear" ‒ BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense
  5. "Be dismayed" ‒ BDB 369, KB 365, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: POSSESS THE LAND

▣
NASB, NRSV, JPSOA  "Do not fear or be dismayed"
NKJV  "do not fear or be discouraged"
TEV  "do not hesitate or be afraid"
NJB, REB  "do not be afraid or discouraged"
Peshitta, LXX  "fear not, neither be terrified"

This prohibition from YHWH was based on their trust in His covenant promises and presence! This phrase occurs twelve times in the OT (e.g. 31:8; Josh. 1:9; 8:10; 10:25; 1 Chr. 22:13; 28:20; 2 Chr. 20:15; 32:7; Jer. 30:10; 46:27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:22 Numbers 13:1-3 is the background for this verse. It recalls Moses' commands to the tribes:

  1. "Send" ‒ BDB 1018, KB 1511, Qal COHORTATIVE
  2. "Search out" ‒ BDB 343, KB 340, Qal IMPERFECT, used in a JUSSIVE sense
  3. "Bring back" ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:23 "I took twelve of your men, one man for each tribe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:23 "I took twelve of your men, one man for each tribe" Moses was smart to try and include each of the tribes so that each one felt included.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:24 "the valley of Eshcol"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:24 "the valley of Eshcol" This term (BDB 79) means "cluster" or "stalk." Numbers 13:23-24 says that they cut one cluster of grapes that was so big that it took two men to carry it on a pole. This is how the valley (or Wadi) got its Hebrew name, but its location in southern Palestine is uncertain, possibly somewhere close to Hebron (cf. Num. 13:22,23).

▣ "spied it out" "Spied" (BDB 920, KB 1183, Piel IMPERFECT with waw) is a variation of the word for "foot" (BDB 919), which implies that they walked through the land. They had no animals to ride and it was a real step of faith for them to walk throughout this land and be seen by its inhabitants.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:25 "It is a good land which the Lord our God is about to give us"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:25 "It is a good land which the Lord our God is about to give us" What a powerful covenantal affirmation! Yet, they did not act on the theological affirmation, but on their fear (e.g. Deut. 1:21).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:26 "rebelled"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:26 "rebelled" The VERB (BDB 598, KB 632, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw) becomes a common word in Deuteronomy (e.g. 1:26,43; 9:7,23,24; 21:18,20; 31:27; and also in the Psalms). Its COGNATE in Aramaic means "to dispute with" and in Syriac, "to contend with." It denotes willful, known disobedience!

▣ "the command of the Lord" The command in Deut. 1:8 and 21 were for them to go up and take the land. The account of the spies and their report is found in Numbers 13.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:27 "you grumbled in your tents"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:27 "you grumbled in your tents" The people were in their tents grumbling (BDB 920, KB 1188, Niphal IMPERFECT with waw); they were not doing it publicly, but God saw their hearts (cf. Ps. 106:25) and knew that they were rebelling against Him (i.e. "slanderous whispers," cf. Prov. 16:28; 18:8; 26:20,22). God knows not only what we say (cf. Deut. 1:25c), but what is in our heart-our motives (cf. Num. 14:1-6; 1 Sam. 2:3; 16:7; 1 Kgs.8:39; 1 Chr. 28:9; 2 Chr. 6:36; Ps. 7:9; 44:21; 94:11; 139:1-4; Prov. 15:11; 20:27; 21:2; Jer. 11:20; 17:9-10; 20:12; Luke 16:15; Acts 1:24; 15:8; Rom. 8:26; 1 John 3:20; Rev. 2:23).

▣ "the Lord hates us" In this verse the people are impugning the motives and nature of YHWH (e.g. Deut. 9:28). They had forgotten all of the wonderful promises and provisions of God during their trek from Sinai to Kadesh and had started focusing on their present situation, which they viewed as devastating.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:28 "Our brethren have made our hearts melt"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:28 "Our brethren have made our hearts melt" The people tried to blame the spies for their unbelief. The term "melt" (BDB 587, KB 606) is imagery for a person becoming fearful and losing the will to resist (cf. Deut. 20:8; Josh. 2:11; 5:1; 7:5; and possibly 14:8).

▣
NASB, REB  "bigger and taller"
NKJV, Peshitta  "greater and taller"
NRSV, TEV, NJB, NIV, JPSOA  "stronger and taller"
NET  "more numerous and taller"
LXX  "great and numerous"

It is obvious from the different translations that the question is about the first term. Is it synonymous or does it add new information?

The ADJECTIVE (BDB 152) basically means "great." It is used of:

  1. great in extent
  2. great in number
  3. great in intensity
  4. great in importance

The term is common and has a wide semantic field. Only context can clarify its meaning. The Septuagint seems to understand these terms as "more populous and mightier" (as does the UBS Text Project, p. 267, but with considerable doubt, a "C" rating). Part of the problem of translation is the place of "giants" in the OT!

SPECIAL TOPIC: GIANTS

▣ "the cities are large and fortified to heaven" From archeology we have found evidence about some of these cities. Lachish was a southern Amorite city which had a wall 29 feet thick. The walls of these cities had an occasional raised turret or tower. One can understand how the Israelites were overwhelmed when they saw these cities ("fortified" BDB 130, KB 148, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE means "inaccessible").

This hyperbole "fortified to heaven" is used in the same figurative sense as the names of the Ziggurats in Babylon (cf. Gen. 11:4).

▣ "Anakim" The word (BDB 778 I) literally means "longneckers." This refers to the giants (cf. Genesis 6 and Egyptian letter Anastasi I). This tribe is identified with southern Canaan, esp. Hebron. Most were killed by Caleb (cf. Josh. 11:21-22).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS (GIANTS), #5

SPECIAL TOPIC: "sons of God" in Genesis 6

1:29
NASB  "Do not be shocked, nor fear them"
NKJV  "do not be terrified, or be afraid of them"
NRSV, JPSOA  "Have no dread or fear of them"
TEV  "Don't be afraid of those people"
NJB  "Do not take fright, do not be afraid of them"
LXX  "Do not be alarmed, neither be afraid of them"
Peshitta  "Fear not, neither tremble of them"

The first VERB (BDB 791, KB 888, Qal IMPERFECT) means "cause to tremble." In Aramaic it means "to quiver" and in Syriac "to come upon accidently or violently" (cf. Deut. 7:21; 20:3; 31:6).

The second VERB (BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT) means "fear" or "awe." This is the common term for fear:

  1. of enemies ‒ Deut. 1:21,29; 2:4; 3:2,22; 7:18,19; 20:1,3; 31:6; Josh. 11:6
  2. peoples of the earth fear the people of God ‒ Deut. 28:10 (cf. Josh. 4:24); Josh. 9:24
  3. Israel is to fear/awe/respect YHWH ‒ Deut. 4:10; 5:5; 6:2,13,24; 10:12,20; 13:11; 14:23; 17:13,19; 19:20; 21:21; 25:18; 28:58; 31:12; Josh. 4:24

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:30 "The Lord your God who goes before you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:30 "The Lord your God who goes before you" This is a powerful encouraging phrase expressing YHWH's best gift—His personal presence and provision. Notice in Deut. 1:30 He goes ahead of them to battle (i.e. the Divine Warrior, cf. Deut. 9:3); in Deut. 1:33 He goes ahead of them to lead them through the desert (i.e. like the shekinah cloud during the wilderness wanderings).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

▣ "fight on your behalf" This is an example of "holy war" or herem (BDB 355, e.g. Deut. 2:24; 3:6; 7:2; 20:16-18; Josh. 6:17,21;8:26;10:1,28,37;11:12, 20-21). This is God's judgment on the Amorites/Canaanites for their sin, not just God favoring His people (cf. Gen. 15:16). God had given the peoples of Canaan many chances to repent, but they would not, so His judgment was upon them. God will also judge His own people when they take up these same Canaanite practices (i.e. the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles)! Here, God is telling His people not to fear but to trust Him because He was on their side (e.g. Deut. 3:22; 20:4; Josh. 10:14,42; 11:5-6)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEREM

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:31 "your God carried you, just as a man carries his son"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:31 "your God carried you, just as a man carries his son" "Carry" (BDB 669, KB 724, Qal PERFECT) can refer to physically bearing someone or something or "sustaining someone." God as Father (i.e. Parent) is a wonderful biblical, personal family imagery (cf. Deut. 8:5; 32:6; Exod. 4:22; Ps. 27:10; 68:5; 103:13; Prov. 3:12; Isa. 1:2; 63:16; Jer. 3:19; Hosea 11:1-4; Mal. 1:6; Acts 13:18).

In the OT "son" is corporate imagery for YHWH's fatherhood for Israel, but it becomes individual to Davidic king and his special royal descendant (i.e. Messiah, Ps. 2:2,7; Acts 13:33).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FATHERHOOD OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:32 "But for all this"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:32 "But for all this" This includes YHWH's special, personal presence and care from the call of Abraham (Genesis 13) through the Exodus (Exodus ‒ Numbers).

▣ "you did not trust the Lord your God" The VERB (BDB 52, KB 63, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) is a major theological term. It is the basis of the personal relationship central to the covenant.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH, AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OLD TESTAMENT

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:33 "who goes before you on your way, to seek out a place for you to encamp, in fire by night and cloud by day, to show you the way in which you should go"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:33 "who goes before you on your way, to seek out a place for you to encamp, in fire by night and cloud by day, to show you the way in which you should go" God went before the people in a fire by night and cloud by day, which is known as the "Shekinah cloud of glory" (e.g. Exod. 13:21-22; 14:19,24; 19:16-18; 20:21; 24:15,18; 33:9-10; Lev. 16:2; Num. 9:15-23; 14:14; Ps. 78:14) This cloud symbolizes the presence or transportation of Deity and is found throughout the Bible (e.g. 1 Kgs. 8:10,12; Ezek. 1:4; Dan. 7:13; Matt. 24:30; 26:64; Acts 1:9-11; 1 Thess. 4:17; Rev. 1:7). He is coming on the clouds!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: COMING ON THE CLOUDS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:34 "He was angry and took an oath"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:34 "He was angry and took an oath" This same phrase, "took an oath" (BDB 989 KB 1396, Niphal IMPERFECT with waw, usually identified by the phrase, "As I live"), was used when YHWH committed Himself to a covenant relationship with Israel. Here He is committing Himself to the covenant consequence for disobedience-cursing. Notice that YHWH's promise to Abraham was to succeeding generations, but the curse was only to one generation, which was the initial evil (i.e. unbelief in YHWH's promise of giving them Canaan) of the generation of the Exodus.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:35
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:35 All of the men of military age (i.e. 20 years and up), who refused to follow YHWH's command and take the land, are punished and the people had to wander in the wilderness until their deaths (i.e. 38 years). The NT book of Hebrews, chapters 3-4, discusses this very issue of faithlessness.

Only the two spies who brought the positive report, Caleb (cf. Deut. 1:36) and Joshua (cf. Deut. 1:38), were excluded. Covenant disobedience results in covenant curses for Israel (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 27-29) and Moses (cf. Deut. 3:26-27).

▣ "the good land" This is a recurrent phrase (cf. Exod. 3:8; Deut. 1:35; 3:25; 4:21,22; 8:7,20; Josh. 23:13). "Good" denoted

  1. God's presence (i.e. God is "good," Ps. 86:5; 100:5; 106:1; 107:1; 118:1,29; 145:9; and also note the parallelism of Amos 5:4,6,14,15)
  2. "a land flowing with milk and honey" (e.g. Exod. 3:8,17; 13:5; 33:3; Num. 13:27; 14:8; 16:13,14; Deut. 6:3; 11:9; 26:9,15; 27:3; 31:20; Josh. 5:6).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:36 "the land on which he has set foot"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:36 "the land on which he has set foot" The land which Caleb will capture and thereby inherit is located around Hebron. We think it is near the valley of Eshcol (cf. Josh. 15:13), where the giants lived!

▣ "fully" This means "wholeheartedly" (BDB 569, KB 583, Piel PERFECT). It refers to one without mixed motives; Caleb loved YHWH with all his heart and followed Him. It is imagery of true devotion (e.g. Num. 14:24; 32:11-12; Josh. 14:8,9,14; 1 Kgs. 11:6). It is theologically parallel to the phrase, "with all your heart and with all your soul" (cf. Deut. 6:5; 10:12; 13:3; 30:2; 1 Kgs. 9:4; 11:4).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:37 "The Lord was angry with me also on your account"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:37 "The Lord was angry with me also on your account" Moses was trying to blame the people for his own disobedience (cf. Deut. 3:26, just as Adam tried to do, cf. Gen. 3:12), but note Num. 20:7-13,24; 27:14; Deut. 4:21.

The VERB "angry" (BDB 60, KB 72, Hithpael PERFECT) is from the NOUN for "nostril" or "nose." Apparently it referred to

  1. the flaring of the nostril as a physical sign of anger
  2. snorting a nasal sound

This term is used consistently for divine (anthropomorphic) anger (cf. Exod. 32:12; Deut. 1:37; 4:21; 9:8,20; 2 Kgs. 24:20).

Another use of this word in connection to deity is the phrase, "slow to anger," which emphasizes God's patience and longsuffering (e.g. Exod. 34:6; Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Prov. 14:29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (ANTHROPOMORPHISM)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:38 "Joshua, son of Nun, who stands before you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:38 "Joshua, son of Nun, who stands before you" The phrase, "who stands before you," is a Hebrew idiom which refers to a leader. Joshua was the right-hand man of Moses and this may be a prophecy of his future leadership role.

▣ "encourage him" This VERB (BDB 304, KB 302, Piel IMPERATIVE) means "make strong" (e.g. 3:28). YHWH Himself does this in Josh. 1:6,7,9,18!

▣ "for he will cause Israel to inherit it" This promise goes back to the prophecies to the Patriarchs (e.g. Genesis 12, 15, 18, 26) about their descendants' possession of Canaan (e.g. 3:28; 31:7; Josh. 11:23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:39 "your little ones who you said would become a prey"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:39 "your little ones who you said would become a prey" This refers to Numbers 14:3,31. Because of the adults' disbelief YHWH is telling them that their children surely would inherit the land just as He had promised.

▣ "who this day have no knowledge of good or evil" Historically this is referring to the children who came out of Egypt. YHWH did not hold them responsible until they were capable of covenant understanding and commitment (e.g. Isa. 7:15).

In this text two sides/poles can be seen in:

  1. "I will give it to them" (God's sovereignty, cf. Deut. 1:8)
  2. "They shall posses it" (human choice and responsibility, cf. Deut. 1:8)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE AGE OF ACCOUNTABILITY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:40 "by the way to the Red Sea"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:40 "by the way to the Red Sea" This seems to be a reference to the road called "the King's Highway" that ran beside the Gulf of Aqaba from Elath to Kadesh-barnea (cf. Num. 14:25; 20:17; 21:22). This does not refer to the Egyptian body of water crossed early in the Exodus, unless it means "in the general direction of."

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE RED SEA

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:41 "We have sinned against the Lord; we will indeed go up and fight"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:41 "We have sinned against the Lord; we will indeed go up and fight" This is apparently consequence-related repentance. Theologically this shows that many times a lost opportunity, because of unbelief, cannot be regained. This context clearly shows that they were still not obeying YHWH (cf. Deut. 1:43). This theological truth is the central focus of many of the OT historical narratives.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:42 "I am not among you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:42 "I am not among you" The key to victory was not their military strength, but the presence of YHWH (cf. Deut. 1:43).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:43
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:43 Notice the parallel descriptions of Israel:

  1. "You would not listen" ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal PERFECT (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR)
  2. "You rebelled against the command" ‒ BDB 598, KB 632, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw
  3. "Acted presumptuously" ‒ BDB 267, KB 268, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw

If Israel would have listened to YHWH earlier and done this very thing they would have successful, but by doing it now it shows their continual self-asserting waywardness!

This context clearly shows that obedience is integrally related to His covenant promises, presence, and power!

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:44 "the Amorites who lived in that hill country"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:44 "the Amorites who lived in that hill country" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE, C. #7.

▣
NASB, JPSOA, REB  "crushed you"
NKJV  "drove you back"
NRSV  "beat you down"
TEV, LXX, Peshitta,  "chased you"
NJB  "pursued you"

The VERB (BDB 510, KB 507, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw) means "to beat into pieces." This event is recorded in Num. 14:45.

The ADJECTIVE was used of beating oil out of olives (cf. Exod. 29:40; Num. 28:5). It is used for the destruction of

  1. the golden calf (cf. Deut. 9:21)
  2. the smashing of idols (cf. Micah 1:7)

▣ "from Seir" Seir refers to the central mountainous region of Edom.

▣
NASB, NKJV, NJB  "to Hormah"
NRSV, TEV  "as far as Hormah"
REB, JPSOA  "at Hormah"
LXX  "as far as Horma"
Peshitta  "as far as Hirmah"

The term (BDB 356) originally referred to a Canaanite city, cf. Num. 21:3). It came to mean "devoted to destruction," the Hebrew concept of herem. The city was originally called Zephath (cf. Jdg. 1:17). After the Israelites destroyed it, they renamed it devoted/destroyed to/for YHWH (like Jericho, Joshua 6-7). It was located in the tribal allocation of Simeon, northeast of Beersheba.
SPECIAL TOPIC: HEREM

The PREPOSITION (BDB 723 III) implies that the Canaanites/Amorites chased the Israelites from Edom (Seir) to this area just northeast of Beersheba, where they totally defeated them! YHWH was not with His rebellious and presumptuous people!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:45 "Then you returned and wept before the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:45 "Then you returned and wept before the Lord" The people wept outwardly, but YHWH knew their hearts. It was sorrow based on consequences, not repentance.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (NT)

▣ "but the Lord did not listen to your voice, nor give ear to you" It was not that YHWH did not hear them, but He did not hearken unto them. He heard them, but said "No." Sin always brings consequences, even forgiven sin!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 1:46 "Kadesh"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:46 "Kadesh" This refers to Kadesh-Barnea, which is the largest oasis in the region and common resting site of carravans. The name "Kadesh" (BDB 873 II) comes from the root "holy" or "separated" (BDB 871). It was about 50 miles south of Beer-Sheba.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What is the basic purpose of Deuteronomy?
  2. Why are Sihon and Og mentioned here briefly when they are discussed fully in Deuteronomy 2 and 3?
  3. List the vital items concerned with the judicial system of Moses?
  4. Where did the giants come from?
  5. Why was God so angry at Israel?
  6. Did Israel's repentance affect God's decision?

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:1 "the wilderness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:1 "the wilderness" There are several "wildernesses" connected to the exodus.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WILDERNESSES OF THE EXODUS

▣ "by the way of the Red Sea" This refers to the Arabah Road (cf. TEV "on the road to the Gulf of Aqaba"), in the Jordan Rift Valley, which runs north and south on both sides of the Dead Sea (cf. Deut. 2:8). It is a wide valley which begins near the cities of Elath or Ezion-geber on the Gulf of Aqaba and goes through the heart of Edom and Moab and the kingdom of the Amorites to Damascus, Syria. In the OT the road is called "the King's Highway" (e.g. Num. 20:17 and 21:22).

The term "Red Sea" (BDB 410 CONSTRUCT with BDB 693) is literally "sea of reeds/weeds." This term is used for

  1. "the unknown and mysterious waters to the south"
  2. the body of water that the Israelites crossed in the exodus and, as here and Deut. 1:40
  3. the body of water called the Gulf of Aqaba on the eastern side of the Sinai Peninsula
  4. In one OT passage the term refers to the Indian Ocean.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE RED SEA

▣ "as the Lord spoke to me" Deuteronomy depicts itself as a revelation from YHWH to Moses (cf. Deut. 2:1,2,9,17,31). YHWH directed His people by:

  1. direct revelation to Moses (cf. Deut. 2:2)
  2. the movement of the Shekinah cloud of glory
  3. the use of the Urim and Thummim (i.e. High Priest)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: URIM AND THUMMIM

▣ "Mount Seir" This refers to the land of Edom (cf. Deut. 2:5; 1:2; Exod. 3:1; 17:6).

▣
NASB, Peshitta  "circled"
NKJV, NRSV, LXX, JPSOA  "skirted"
TEV  "wandering"
NJB  "gone far away"

This VERB (BDB 685, KB 738, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT in Deut. 2:3 and a Qal IMPERFECT with waw in Deut. 2:1) means "turn about," "go around," "surround." The Israelites had no clear direction because of the evil unbelieving generation. They wandered around Kadesh-barnea for thirty-eight years, but YHWH is about to give specific, clear directions to Moses. The VERB "go around" or "skirt" fits this text best.

▣ "Now turn north" This may refer to Numbers 20, where Israel asked if they could pass through the land of Edom, but the Edomites would not let them. They then asked to pass through the land of the Moabites, and they also said no. This is recording an early event (cf. ICC p. 34). Here they are asking if they could go up the King's Highway, which ran through the center of these countries. They were willing to buy food and water, but the Edomites and the Moabites (the Israelites' relatives through Lot and Esau) said, "No." Rather than go through Edom, they went around their border.

Like so many Hebrew terms, this one (BDB 815, KB 937) has a concrete, literal meaning (e.g. here) and a developed, metaphorical meaning. "Turn" is the Hebrew term often translated "repent" (e.g. 2 Kgs. 17:13; 2 Chr. 30:6; Isa. 44:22; Jer. 3:11-4:2; Hosea 14:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)
