READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BRIEF OUTLINE OF CHAPTER 2

  1. Israel's relations with Edom, Deut. 2:4-7

  2. Israel's relations with Moab, Deut. 2:8-15

  3. Israel's relations with Ammon, Deut. 2:16-19

  4. Deuteronomy 2:20-23 is a parenthesis related to the Rephaim (See SPECIAL TOPIC: GIANTS)

  5. Israel's relations with Amorites on the eastern bank of Jordan, Deut. 2:24-37

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:4 "command"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4 "command" This term (BDB 845, KB 1010, Piel IMPERATIVE), like "turn" (BDB 815, KB 937, Qal IMPERATIVE) in Deut. 2:3, shows that Moses is recording the very commands of YHWH (as does the Hithpael IMPERFECT used as a JUSSIVE in Deut. 2:5, "do not provoke them"). He personally directed their journey.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION

▣
NASB, LXX  "your brothers"
NKJV, Peshitta  "your brethren"
NRSV  "your kindred"
TEV  "your distant relatives"
NJB, REB, JPSOA  "your kinsmen"

The English translation shows the implications of the Hebrew word "brother" (BDB 26). It is used several times of Edom (descendants of Esau, cf. Num. 20:14; Deut. 2:4,8; Obad. v. 10).

▣ "they will be afraid of you" This is a prophetic statement which goes back to the Song of Deliverance in which Miriam praises God for the miraculous Reed Sea crossing. YHWH predicted that "Edom and Moab would be terrified of the Israelites" (cf. Exod. 15:15).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:4, 9, 19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4, 9, 19 Throughout this chapter there are several noteworthy phrases connected to God's sovereignty:

  1. "I will not give" (Deut. 2:5, 9, 19)
  2. "I have given" (Deut. 2:5, 9)
  3. "the Lord gave" (Deut. 2:12)
  4. "the Lord our God is giving to us" (Deut. 2:29)
  5. "God delivered him over to us" (Deut. 2:33)

This chapter shows the sovereignty of YHWH in international boundaries (cf. Deut. 32:8 [LXX]; Neh. 9:22), because each of these phrases stresses that YHWH is the one who gave the land to certain people groups to inherit. This chapter shows that YHWH did not exclusively give land to Israel, but He gave some to every nation. Some lost their land because of their sins (e.g. Gen. 15:16) and Israel also lost her land for a period (i.e. Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian exiles) because of her sin. This is asserting that YHWH is the universal God. In a day of polytheism, this is a wonderful statement of monotheism. There is one and only one God, Deut. 6:4-6. He is the One who gives the land even to the Edomites, Moabites, Amorites, etc. (esp. Deut. 32:8 in the Septuagint [LXX]).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

▣
NASB, NRSV, REB  "So be very careful"
NKJV  "Therefore watch yourselves carefully"
TEV  "but you must not start a war" (combines
  this phrase with the next one in v. 5)
NJB  "and you will be well protected"
LXX  "they will be very cautious"
Peshitta  "take heed to yourselves"

The literal phrase is "so take good heed" (a CONJUNCTION, VERB [BDB 1036, KB 1581, Niphal PERFECT], and ADVERB [BDB 547]). The Septuagint is similar to TEV.

This phrase, in various forms, is used several times in Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 2:4; 4:9,15,23; 6:12; 8:11; 11:16; 12:13,19,30; 15:9; 24:8). It implies, "keep your mind alert," "watch what you are doing," "think clearly about the implications of your actions," and "do not provoke them."

2:5
NASB  "even as little as a footstep"
NKJV  "not so much as one footstep"
NRSV, NJB  "even so much as a foot's length"
TEV  "as much as a square foot"
LXX  "a foot's pace"
Peshitta  "not so much as the breadth of a foot"

This is a rare Hebrew term (BDB 204). It refers to a stepping place. The same root is used in Deut. 11:24 and Josh. 1:3. In a sense this was an encouraging word from YHWH. He had given land to both Edom and Moab. It was theirs, every inch of it! He was in the process of giving land to Israel. His land grant gifts were secure.

Now it must be added that eventually, because of sin, these nations (i.e. Edom and Moab) lost their land and perished as a people. All land gifts were conditional. This is also true of Israel (i.e. the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles). All of YHWH's covenants (except Genesis 6 and 15) are conditional.

His promises of redemption are sure (unconditional), but each person/nation must respond and continue to respond appropriately! A continuing, obedient faith relationship is crucial. YHWH requires faith, repentance, obedience, and perseverance, in both the OT and the NT.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:6 Israel was to purchase both food and water as a gesture of their recognition of Edom's sovereignty over their land, which was given by YHWH.

  1. "Buy food" (BDB 991, KB 1404, Qal IMPERFECT)
  2. "Purchase water" (BDB 500, KB 497, Qal IMPERFECT)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:7 "These forty years the Lord your God has been with you; you have not lacked a thing"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:7 "These forty years the Lord your God has been with you; you have not lacked a thing" This passage describes the love of YHWH even in the midst of Israel's rebellion against Him (i.e. lack of faith in His promise to give them the land of Canaan).

The Wilderness Wandering Period (lit. 38 years, cf. Deut. 2:14) was a judgment to a generation of Israelites with little faith, but it turned into a time of YHWH's personal presence and provision. The rabbis call it the honeymoon period between YHWH and Israel. YHWH provided (cf. Det. 8:3-4; 29:5-6):

  1. protection
  2. personal guidance
  3. food
  4. water
  5. clothes that did not wear out
  6. victory in battle

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:8 "So we passed beyond our brothers, the sons of Esau who live in Seir"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:8 "So we passed beyond our brothers, the sons of Esau who live in Seir" This use of "brothers" is somewhat ironic. They were kin. They did come from the same ancestors, Isaac and Rebekah, but they were acting like anything except relatives.

"Seir" refers to the mountain range in the country of Edom. So "Seir" and "Edom" are synonymous.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:8 27 "Arabah road"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:8 27 "Arabah road" This refers to "the Kings Highway," from the Gulf of Aqaba to Damascus, which was a major trade route (see full note at Deut. 2:1. Also note Num. 20:17,19; 21:22).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:8 "Elath"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:8 "Elath" This is literally a port city called "palm trees" (BDB 19). This is probably close to Ezion-geber (cf. 1 Kgs. 9:26), which is at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba. It was where the King's Highway from Damascus stopped.

▣ "Ezion-geber" This location is mentioned in Num. 33:35. It was also a port on the Gulf of Aqaba (cf. 1 Kgs. 9:26).

▣ "the way of the wilderness of Moab" The Macmillan Bible Atlas, map 10, shows this desert road as parallel to "the King's Highway," but to the east. The southern end passes through Edom and is known as "the way of the wilderness of Edom" (cf. 2 Kgs. 3:8). The King's Highway and this smaller desert road meet at Rabbath-bene-ammon, which is to the east of Jericho.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:9 "Do not harass Moab, nor provoke them to war"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:9 "Do not harass Moab, nor provoke them to war" This is parallel to Deut. 2:5 about Edom. The terms are different, but the thought is the same.

Both of the VERBS are JUSSIVES:

  1. "harass" (BDB 849 III, KB 1015, Qal JUSSIVE, cf. Exod. 23:22; Esther 8:11)
  2. "provoke" (BDB 173, KB 202, Hithpael JUSSIVE, Deut. 2:19,24; Prov. 28:4; Dan. 11:10)

▣ "Ar" This is either a reference to Moab in general or its capital city (i.e. "Ar" in Moabite means "city," cf. Num. 21:15,28; Deut. 2:9,18,29; Isa. 15:1). It was located on the left bank of the Arnon River in mountainous Moab.

▣ "sons of Lot as a possession" See the account of Lot's life in Gen. 19:37-38.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:10-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:10-12 These verses are an editorial comment, as are Deut. 2:20-23; 3:9,11,13-14. The following are all terms for giants:

  1. Emim (BDB 34 which is from the root "terror" or "dread," Deut. 2:10,11; Gen. 14:6)
  2. Anakim (BDB 778, which means "long-neck," Deut. 2:10,11,21)
  3. Rephaim (Deut. 2:11,20)

These terms can mean either

  1. large or tall in size
  2. of a particular ethnic origin
  3. later in Isaiah and Jeremiah, it is used for the realm of the dead. Here it probably refers to size

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS (Giants)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:12 "Horites"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:12 "Horites" There is some debate concerning the relation between the Horites (BDB 360) and the Hurrians (ABD, vol. 3, pp. 335-338). I do not think that they are the same (ABD, vol. 3, p. 288). I believe there were two different peoples, although there is no way to be dogmatic (NET Bible, p. 348 #5). The Horites were a tribal group that lived in the region of Edom/Seir before Edom was a nation (cf. Gen. 14:6; 36:20-30).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:13 "Now arise and cross over"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:13 "Now arise and cross over" These two VERBS (BDB 877, KB 1086 and BDB 716, KB 778) are both Qal IMPERATIVES. YHWH is still telling Moses exactly what to do.

▣ "brook Zered" This is the name of a wadi between Moab and Edom (cf. Num. 21:12). A wadi is a silt-filled ravine where water runs during the rainy season, a seasonal brook, not a river. The silt often forms a "road." It formed the border between Edom and Moab.

The meaning of the term "Zered" (BDB 279) is unknown.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:14, 16 "all the generation of the men of war"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:14, 16 "all the generation of the men of war" The "men of war" included every male between 20 and 50 years of age (cf. Exod. 30:14; 38:26; Num. 1:3; 14:29). All of this evil unbelieving generation (i.e. lack of faith in YHWH's promises) had to die (cf. Deut. 2:15) before the younger Israelis could possess the Promised Land.

▣ "as the Lord had sworn" See Num. 14:28-29; Deut. 1:34-35.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:14 "Now the time that it took for us. . .was thirty-eight years"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:14 "Now the time that it took for us. . .was thirty-eight years" This is a summary verse of the wilderness wandering period (cf. Deut. 2:7).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:15 "the hand of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:15 "the hand of the Lord" This text brings up the question, "Did the men of fighting age (20-50 years old) die of natural causes or the judgment of YHWH ("the hand of the Lord")?

  1. theologically, it was the judgment of YHWH (Jewish Study Bible, p. 367)
  2. pratically, because of the 38 years that it took for all of them to die, it was natural causes

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (ANTHROPOMORPHISM)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:16 "all the men of war had finally perished"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:16 "all the men of war had finally perished" This shows a balance between the love of God and the justice of God. God's purpose is not just to punish, but to help His people learn from their mistakes. Therefore, He made these people, under His death sentence, wander around for 38 years, but He fed them, He loved them and He provided for them. It wasn't sudden death, but it was an untimely death. Everyone of the men who came up to Kadesh-barnea, 20 years of age and up, were now dead, except Joshua and Caleb.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:19 This is parallel to Deut. 2:5 and 2:9. These are the same VERBS as Deut. 2:9. Here the first (BDB 849, KB 1015) is JUSSIVE in meaning, but not form. The second (BDB 173, KB 202) is a Hithpael JUSSIVE. The Ammonites were also relatives of the Israelites through Lot.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:20 "(It is also regarded as the land of the Rephaim)"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:20 "(It is also regarded as the land of the Rephaim)" This was an ethnic group who lived in this place. They were also called Zamzummin. Verse 21 shows us they were part of the giants (cf. Deut. 2:9).

▣ "Zamzummin" See Genesis 14:5 and SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS (Giants).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:21 YHWH had been faithful to the descendants of Esau (Deut. 2:5,22) and Lot (Deut. 2:9-10, 21-22). The same "holy war" vocabulary used to describe Israel's victories of conquest are used to describe Edom and Ammon's conquest of their tribal lands.

2:23
NASB, NRSV, TEV, REB, JPSOA  "Avvim"
NKJV  "Avim"
NJB, Peshitta  "Avvites"
LXX  "Hevites"

This term (BDB 732) has two meanings:

  1. A people group which inhabited the land south of Palestine. They were conquered by Aegean people (i.e. Philistines). Albright even associates them with Hyksos settlements (cf. ABD, vol. 1, p. 531). This chapter has listed original inhabitants of places who were defeated and dispossessed.
  2. Later in Joshua this term becomes the name of a city in the tribal allocation of Benjamin (cf. Josh. 18:23). Some scholars have surmised that they were people from Ai.

▣ "the Caphtorim who came from Caphtor" This term (BDB 499) could possibly be the island of Crete (JPSOA), Cyprus, Cappadocia, or northern Egypt (cf. Gen. 10:13-14). We do not know exactly. The Caphtorim (plural of Caphtor) were possibly neighbors or relatives of the Philistines (cf. Gen. 10:14; Jer. 47:4; Amos 9:7).

R. K. Harrison, Old Testament Times, pp. 96-97, asserts the "Caphtorim" were part of the Hyksos, who invaded Egypt (1720-1570 B.C.). Therefore, they were Semites, possibly related to the "Habiru."

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW PEOPLE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:24 This verse has several commands:

  1. "Arise" ‒ BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Gen. 13:17
  2. "Set out" ‒ BDB 652, KB 704, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Deut. 1:19; 2:1
  3. "Pass through" ‒ BDB 716, KB 778, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Isa. 23:12
  4. "Look" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE
  5. "Begin" ‒ BDB 320 III, KB 319, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Deut. 2:31
  6. "To take possession" ‒ BDB 439, KB 441, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Det. 1:8,21; 2:31; 9:23
  7. "Contend" ‒ BDB 173, KB 202, Hithpael IMPERATIVE, cf. Deut. 2:5,9,19; Dan. 11:10

YHWH is commanding, encouraging, and challenging His people to trust Him and obey His word as their parents did not. The land was theirs if they exercised faith (i.e. a conditional aspect)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: POSSESS THE LAND

▣ "Amorite" See note at Deut. 1:4. The capital of this kingdom was Heshbon. It became the allotted tribal territory of Reuben.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:25 "I will begin to put"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:25 "I will begin to put" These two terms are IMPERATIVES in Deut. 2:24. God was ready to act as warrior on their behalf if they would trust Him and enter into battle with the local inhabitants!

▣ "dread and fear" The first term (BDB 808) means "to be in awe" or "dread":

  1. Israel's enemies will dread them ‒ Deut. 2:25; 11:25; Ps. 105:38
  2. the Israelis will be afraid of YHWH if they sin ‒ Deut. 28:66,67
  3. YHWH is to be awed ‒ Ps. 119:120

The second term (BDB 432) means "to fear":

  1. the fear of God ‒ Exod. 20:20
  2. reverence of God ‒ Ps. 2:11; 5:7; 90:11; 119:38
  3. fear of death ‒ Ps. 55:4-5
  4. fear of Israel ‒ Deut. 2:25

▣ "everywhere under the heavens" This is an obvious hyperbole (i.e. whole earth, 4:19; Dan. 9:12). This is referring to the inhabitants of Canaan. See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, chapter 5, "Hebrew Idiom and Hebrew Thought."

▣ "tremble and be in anguish" This is parallel to "dread and fear." The first VERB (BDB 919, KB 1182, Qal PERFECT with waw) means "quake" or "quiver" (cf. Prov. 29:9; Isa. 14:9).

The second VERB (BDB 296, KB 297, Qal PERFECT with waw) means "dance," "whirl" (cf. Lam. 4:6) or "writhe" (cf. Isa. 23:4; 26:18 [giving birth]).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:26 "Kedemoth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:26 "Kedemoth" This (BDB 870) refers to an area (or settlement) north of the Arnon River, but exactly where is uncertain. This later became a Levitical city in the tribal allocation of Reuben (cf. Josh. 21:37).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:27 "Let me pass through your land, I will travel only on the highway"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:27 "Let me pass through your land, I will travel only on the highway" The first VERB (BDB 716, KB 778, Qal COHORTATIVE) is used often in this historical summary (cf. Deut. 2:4,8,13,14,18,24,27,28, 29,30; 3:18,21,25,27,28; 4:14,21,22,26).

Another textual feature is that the Hebrew word 'way" or "road," with the PREPOSITION is doubled. This is a way of emphasizing that they would not deviate off the main highway. This refers to the King's Highway, which goes through Edom, Moab, and the Kingdom of Sihon (see full note at Deut. 2:1). Moses asserts that they had passed through these kingdoms without causing trouble even when their king would not let Israel pass through. This was the very same offer (cf. Deut. 2:29) that Moses made to Edom (cf. Deut. 2:6).

▣ "I will not turn aside to the right or to the left" Notice Moses is speaking in a corporate sense. Much of the misunderstanding of the Bible can be attributed to the loss of the corporate nature of biblical revelation versus the individual focus of modern, western societies. The rights and privileges of the individual have eclipsed the social collectiveness of the OT.

The phrase is based on the OT idiom of biblical faith as a path or way (e.g. Ps. 119:105). YHWH's will is clearly marked. This concept is literal here (i.e. a highway). So the phrase, "turn to the right or left" is literal. Usually this is used as imagery for the spiritual life (e.g. Num. 20:17; 22:26; Deut. 5:32; 17:11,20; 28:14; Josh. 1:7; 23:6; 1 Kgs. 22:2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WAY.. .THE PATH

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:30 "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:30 "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" The first VERB (BDB 904, KB 1151, Hiphil PERFECT) means "to be hard" in the sense of stubbornness or stiffneckedness:

  1. the Qal IMPERFECT is used in Deut. 1:17; 15:18
  2. the Hiphil is used in Exod. 7:3; 13:15 in relation to YHWH hardening Pharaoh's heart just before the exodus
  3. the Hiphil is used in Deut. 10:16 of YHWH warning the Israelites not to harden their hearts or not to be stiffnecked

Number 2 is a parallel to this context's divine hardening of Sihon's heart (i.e. will).

The second VERB (BDB 54, KB 69, Piel PERFECT) means "to be strong." It is usually used in a positive sense (cf. Deut. 3:28; 31:6,7,23), but here it is used parallel to "stiffnecked" (cf. Deut. 15:7; 2 Chr. 36:13).

This is similar to what happened to Pharaoh:

  1. God hardened his heart (cf. Exod. 7:3; 9:12; 10:1,20,27; 11:10; 14:4,8,17)
  2. Pharaoh hardened his own heart (cf. Exod. 8:15,32; 9:34)

These verses show both God's sovereignty and mankind's God-given free will. The context implies that Pharaoh (in Exodus) and Sihon (in Deuteronomy) had a free will or why would Moses take the time to offer a peace initiative to them? The implication is that YHWH is in control of all things. YHWH set up the circumstances, but they refused (see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 142-143).

Romans 9 and 10 show this same paradox. Chapter 9 focuses on the sovereignty of God while chapter 10 has several universal offers (cf. Rom. 2:4, "everyone"; Rom. 2:11,13, "whosoever"; Rom. 2:12, "all" [twice]).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEART

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD HARDENED

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:31 Three of the IMPERATIVES of Deut. 2:24 are repeated:

  1. "See" ‒ BDB 906, KB 115, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "Begin" ‒ BDB 320, KB 319, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  3. "Occupy" ‒ BDB 439, KB 441, Qal IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:32 "came out to meet us"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:32 "came out to meet us" Sihon lost because he left his fortified cities and was defeated on the plains. This is a good example of where YHWH used human pride to accomplish His purpose (i.e. Pharaoh in the Exodus).

▣ "Jahaz" The exact site is uncertain, but it (BDB 397) is on the eastern side of Jordan in the kingdom of Sihon and probably south of the capital, Heshbon, because the Israelites were coming from the south.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:33 "God delivered him over to us"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:33 "God delivered him over to us" As in Deut. 2:31, YHWH's sovereignty (Deut. 2:32a, "God delivered" BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) and human freedom (Deut. 2:32b, "we defeated" BDB 645, KB 697, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw) are both plainly asserted.

▣ "his sons" The MT has the SINGULAR but the Masoretic scholars suggested it be read as a PLURAL (Qere). From time to time these producers of the MT gave their textual suggestions in their notes. This was an early form of textual criticism.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:34 "We left no survivor"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:34 "We left no survivor" This was a tenet of holy war (herem, BDB 355 I, cf. Deut. 3:6; 7:1-2). All were killed because these people had been sinful for a long time (cf. Deut. 7:16; 20:14). Genesis 15:16 says that "the sin of the Amorite is not yet full" and, therefore, YHWH had waited a long time for them to respond to Him. They did not repent and judgment finally came. If they had not been destroyed, they would have corrupted the worship and theology given on Mt. Sinai. "Holy War' was a judgment and a protective hedge!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CURSE (OT)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:35 "We took only the animals as our booty and the spoil of the cities"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:35 "We took only the animals as our booty and the spoil of the cities" Here is an example of a limited ban (e.g. 3:6-7; Josh. 8:2,27; 11:14). They could take some spoils after they destroyed the people. This was a part of the OT concept of holy war. The battle belonged to YHWH and so, too, the spoils (e.g. Jericho, Joshua 7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEREM

2:36
NASB, Peshitta  "the city which is in the valley"
NKJV, LXX  "the city that is in the ravine"
NRSV, JPSOA  "the town that is in the wadi itself"
TEV  "the city in the middle of that Valley"
NJB  "the town down in the valley"

The variety in the English translations shows the possibilities. For me, a city would never have been built in a wadi because of the danger of flash floods, so valley seems best. This valley is very wide!

▣ "no city that was too high for us" YHWH's people had balked because the cities were too well fortified, the inhabitants were too tall. Now the Israelites are saying, "Those people are big, but we will do it with YHWH's help" (cf. Deut. 1:28).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 2:37
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:37 The area of conquest was very precise (by divine command, cf. Deut. 2:5,9,19).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Follow the route of the conquest on a map.
  2. Who were the giants?
  3. How does one deal with Deut. 2:34?

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:1 "up. . .road"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:1 "up. . .road" This refers to the King's Highway. This was a trans-Jordan road which went directly through the center of Edom, Moab, and Ammon. It was a major caravan route from the Gulf of Aqaba to Damascus (see full note at Deut. 2:1).

▣ "Bashan" The name means "smooth" (BDB 143), in the sense of prime agricultural land (i.e. no rocks). This was a very fertile and wooded land in the northern trans-Jordan area north of the Yarmuk River or possibly Jabbok River to just south of the foothills of Mt. Hermon, which means it included part of the area known as Gilead. It was known for its timber and large herds of cattle.

▣ "Og, king of Bashan" See Num. 21:33-35; Deut. 1:4. He is not mentioned in any ANE text outside the Bible.

▣ "at Edrei" This city (BDB 204) is located on a fork of the Yarmuk River and was one of the royal residences. The capital was Ashtaroth to the north. Og faced Israel here, probably using the river as a defensive position.

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:2 "the Lord said to me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:2 "the Lord said to me" See note at Deut. 2:2.

▣ "Do not fear him" The VERB (BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense) is used often in Deuteronomy (e.g. 1:19,21,29; 2:4; 3:2,22; 4:10). YHWH was fighting in their behalf (i.e. holy war, e.g. Num. 21:34; Josh. 10:8; 11:6).

▣
NASB, NKJV, REB, Peshitta  "I have delivered him"
NRSV  "I have handed him over to you"
TEV  "I am going to give him"
NJB  "I have put him at your mercy"
LXX  "I have given him over into
  your hands"

The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT) means "give," "put," or "set." It is a common VERB. Notice its use in this literary unit of Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 1:8,15,20,21,25,27,35,36,39; 2:5,9,12,19,24,25, 28,29,30,31,33,36; 3:2,3,12,13,15,16,18,19,20; 4:1,8,21,38,40). YHWH is the giver. There is only one God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

▣ "we smote them until no survivor was left" This is the language and reality of "holy war." This reflects the Hebrew concept of herem, or "under the ban" (cf. Deut. 3:6). The following is a representative sample of OT references to this term which shows how it was used in different ways. The concept of herem or "holy war," "ban," or "corban":

  1. total destruction-nothing that breathes is left alive, nothing material can be taken out (cf. Deut. 20:16-18; 1 Sam. 15:3; Joshua 7)
  2. kill all the people, but leave the cattle (cf. Deut. 2:34, 35; 3:6, 7)
  3. kill only the men (cf. Deut. 20:10-15)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CURSE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:4 "region of Argob"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:4 "region of Argob" The term "region" (BDB 286) literally means, "a cord," it is used of:

  1. a cord rope
  2. a measuring line
  3. a piece of land (i.e. region, cf. Josh. 17:5, or inheritance, cf. Deut. 32:9; Josh. 17:14)
  4. a group of people (i.e. band of prophets, cf. 1 Sam. 10:5,10)

▣ "Argob" This term (BDB 918) is the name of a region or plot of land. Its location is in the land of Bashan (cf. Deut. 3:4,13,14; 1 Kgs. 4:13). The root may be related to "clod" (BDB 918) or "heap" (BDB 918), but this is uncertain.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:5 "All these cities were fortified with high walls, gates and bars"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:5 "All these cities were fortified with high walls, gates and bars" These cities were built from volcanic rock blocks and were quite large. They presented a rather intimidating sight. Their size may have reflected the population of the race of people living there. However, the faith of the Israelites was stronger than their fear of the giants (cf. Deut. 2:20-24).

The Handbook for Translators on Deuteronomy from the United Bible Societies mentions that "gates and bars" probably refers to a double gate with a metal bar across both, pp. 68-69. This may explain the PLURAL "gates":

  1. PLURAL as imagery for "strength"
  2. there may just be more than one gate
  3. this may have been the characteristic inner and outer gates (i.e. chambers)
3:6
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, LXX, Peshitta  "utterly destroyed"
TEV  "destroyed"
NJB  "the curse of destruction"
REB  "under solemn ban"
JPSOA  "doomed"

This VERB (BDB 355, KB 353) is used twice in this verse (Hiphil IMPERATIVE and Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE). Its basic meaning is to devote something to YHWH whereby it becomes too holy for human use and must be destroyed. It is regularly used in "holy war" contexts (cf. Deut. 2:34; 7:1-2; Exod. 22:20; Josh. 6:17,21) to assert that the victory and, thereby the spoils belong to YHWH. In these conquest contexts the things devoted to God are the Canaanites and their property. They are judged because of their abominable sins and unwillingness to repent (cf. Gen. 15:16; Lev. 18:24-26; Deut. 9:5).

For a good discussion of "holy war" see Ancient Israel, by Roland deVaux, vol. 1, pp. 258-267.

SPECIAL TOPIC: UTTERLY DESTROY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:8 "Thus we took the land. . .from the hand of the two kings"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:8 "Thus we took the land. . .from the hand of the two kings" Verse 24 says it was "the strong hand of God," which, anthropomorphically (see SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN) shows the power and might of God. Here again is the interplay between God's sovereignty and human effort.

▣ "Mount Hermon" Mount Hermon (BDB 249 CONSTRUCT BDB 356) was the northern limit of the land that YHWH gave to the Israelites. It is the largest mountain in the entire area located in Lebanon, north of the Sea of Chinnereth (i.e. Galilee). Its name (BDB 356) is related to herem (devoted thing) and the site of many temples (cf. Ancient Israel, Roland deVaux, vol. 1, pp. 279-282). It is the northern limit of the conquered lands (cf. Jdgs. 1:1).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:9 "Sidonians"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:9 "Sidonians" This (BDB 851) was the name of a major city in ancient Phoenicia (cf. 1 Kgs. 16:31). It was located on the coast north of Tyre, which later became the major city. It being mentioned instead of Tyre shows the ancientness of this text.

▣ "Sirion" This term (BDB 976, Ps. 29:6) used for Mt. Hermon has been found in Ugaritic texts also shows the ancientness of this text.

▣ "Senir" This term (BDB 972, cf. 1 Chr. 5:23; Song of Songs 4:8; Ezek. 27:5) has been found in accounts of Shalmaneser III, an Assyrian king who attacked Damascus. It is the Amorite name for Mt. Hermon.

3:10
NASB, TEV  "the plateau"
NKJV, Peshitta  "the plain"
NRSV, NJB, REB, JPSOA  "the tableland"
LXX  "Misor"

This term (BDB 449) means "a level place." It could refer to a plain or a flat tableland. Here it refers to the plateau between the Arnon River and the city of Heshbon (cf. Deut. 4:43; Josh. 13:9,16,17,21; Jer. 48:8,21). This plateau was part of Moab and became the tribal inheritance of Reuben (cf. Josh. 20:8).

▣ "Gilead" The term (BDB 166) is of unknown origin or meaning. A popular (word play) definition is given in Gen. 31:48. It can refer to:

  1. a tribe (e.g. Num. 26:29; Jdg. 5:17)
  2. a land (e.g. Gen. 37:25)

It always refers to an area on the east side of the Jordan River from the Arnon River north to the land of Bashan.

▣ "Salecah" This city (BDB 699) seems to form the southeastern limit of Bashan and is often used, along with Mt. Hermon, to designate the extent of Bashan (cf. Josh. 12:5; 13:11; 1 Chr. 5:11).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:11 This seems to be an editorial comment, like Deut. 2:10-12,20; 3:9.

▣ "Rephaim" This can mean

  1. an ethnic group
  2. giants
  3. the realm of the dead

The context here seems to speak of the giants.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS (Giants)

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta, JPSOA  "his bedstead was an iron
  bedstead"
NRSV, NJB, LXX  "his bed, an iron bed"
TEV  "his coffin, made of stone"
REB  "his sarcophagus of basalt"

The term (BDB 793) basically means "a wooden frame." It could be used of a trellis, couch, bed, saddle, chair/throne. Here it refers to a place to sleep. At this period iron was new and precious.

  1. bed ‒ 2 Sam. 17:28; Job 7:13; Ps. 6:6; 41:3; Amos 6:4
  2. couch ‒ Prov. 7:16
  3. coffin (sarcophagus, i.e. one's final place of rest/sleep)

It is possible that "iron" refers to basalt stone sarcophagus color (cf. NET Bible, p. 350). NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 741, says, "there is no literary support for the suggestion this was a sarcophagus or dolmen."

▣ "Rabbah" This (BDB 913) was the capital of the kingdom of Ammon (cf. Josh. 13:25). It is today the capital of Jordan, Amman.

▣ "an ordinary cubit" This is literally, "to the cubit of a man," which was an idiom for a "standard cubit," not a "royal cubit."

This measurement would make the bed 13' by 6'.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CUBIT

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:12 "Reubenites and Gadites"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:12 "Reubenites and Gadites" These two tribes took over Sihons' kingdom (cf. Josh. 13:15-23,24-28).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:13 "half-tribe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:13 "half-tribe" The two sons of Joseph made up the half-tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim (cf. Gen. 41:50,52; 48:1-7). Manasseh's inheritance was split, half on the eastern side of Jordan and half on the western side.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:14 "Jair"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:14 "Jair" Rather than "son of" this means "descendant of" (cf. Num. 32:41). Several of the generations are skipped in this lineage. Verses 12-13 are general in nature and Deut. 3:14-17 provide more detail (cf. NIC, Deuteronomy, Craigie, p. 121).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "SONS OF. . ."

▣ "the son of Manasseh" "Son" here means descendant rather than direct son (cf. 1 Chr. 2:22).

▣ "Geshurites and Maachathites" These are different racial and ethnic groups (BDB 178 and BDB 591). They lived on the northern border of the land of Bashan (cf. Josh. 13:13). Israel did not fight these people.

▣ "Havoth-jair" This can refer to a "town," "region," or "kingdom" (BDB 795 II) of Jair.

▣ "as it is to this day" This phrase refers to a later period than the event (cf. Deut. 2:22; 3:14; 4:38; 10:8,15; 29:28; Josh. 7:26; 8:28,29; 9:27; 13:13; 14:14; 16:10; 22:3,17; 23:8; Jdg. 1:21,26; 10:4; 18:12,30; 19:30). Verse 5 seems to have a similar thrust. The issue is "how much" later. It can refer to "soon after" (e.g. Josh. 6:25; 23:9) or it can mean generations later. Who recorded Moses words? Who arranged the Pentateuch? Who was the final editor? Modern scholarship cannot answer these questions!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PENTATEUCH

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:15 "To Machir"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:15 "To Machir" Numbers 32:39-40 gives more information about this man.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:17 "Arabah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:17 "Arabah" This was another word for the Jordan Valley, which goes from above the Sea of Galilee past the Dead Sea down to the Gulf of Aqaba in the Sinai Peninsula (see note at Deut. 1:1). This is a geological rift through which the Jordan River runs, from the foothills of Mt. Hermon to the Dead Sea.

▣ "Chinnereth" This (BDB 490) is the name of a city in Galilee which was close to a large lake that goes by several names in the Bible:

  1. Chinnereth (e.g. Num. 34:11; Josh. 12:3; 13:27)
  2. Galilee (e.g. Matt. 4:18; Mark 1:16; John 6:1)
  3. Gennesaret (e.g. Luke 5:1)
  4. Tiberias (e.g. John 6:1; 21:1)

▣ "the sea of the Arabah" This lake (cf. Deut. 4:49; Josh. 3:16; 12:3) is also called

  1. "Sea of the Plain" in 2 Kgs. 14:25 is another name for the Salt Sea (cf. Gen. 14:3; Num. 34:3,12; Josh. 3:16; 15:2,5; 18:19)
  2. as it is called today, the Dead Sea
  3. "the eastern sea" (cf. Ezek. 47:18; Joel 2:20; Zech. 14:8)
  4. just "the sea" (cf. Isa. 16:8; Jer. 48:32)

▣ "Pisgah" This mountain (BDB 820) is identified with or is very close to Mt. Nebo (BDB 612 I, cf. Deut. 32:49; 34:1). Possibly they are twin peaks of one formation or the name of the ridge and its highest peak. These mountains are the result of erosion of the plateau of Moab above the Arabah. This name is more common in the OT than Nebo (cf. Num. 21:20; 23:14; Deut. 3:17,27; 4:49; 34:1).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:18 "The Lord your God has given you this land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:18 "The Lord your God has given you this land" This refers to the eastern bank (trans-Jordan) of the Arabah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: POSSESS THE LAND

▣ "shall cross over armed before your brothers" Because Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh settled on the eastern side of the Jordan which had already been conquered, their young men were now to go into battle first and fight for their brothers' land (cf. Deut. 3:19-20) before they could settle in their own land.

▣ "sons of Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:19 "much livestock"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:19 "much livestock" The "much livestock" which they had were the spoils of war both from

  1. Egypt
  2. the trans-Jordan nations

▣ "which I have given you" The source of all blessings is YHWH (the often used VERB "given," BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT). They had not earned the spoils of war themselves.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:20 "the Lord gives rest to your fellow countrymen"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:20 "the Lord gives rest to your fellow countrymen" The book of Hebrews is the best NT commentary on the Pentateuch. In Hebrews 4, the word "rest" is used three ways:

  1. a seventh day rest as God rested after creation, the Sabbath
  2. the Israelites rested after they conquered the Promised Land (cf. Deut. 12:10; 25:19; Josh. 23:1)
  3. heaven, the eternal seventh-day rest

Here "rest" refers to security, #2.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:21 Because of YHWH's provision in the wilderness and victories in the trans-Jordan, the Israelis are to trust Him and march on!

▣ "Joshua" This man became Moses' trusted helper and military leader. His name (BDB 221) in Hebrew is a combination of "YHWH" and "save." A VERB must be added, "YHWH saves," "YHWH brings salvation," "salvation is of YHWH." The Aramaic form of this name is "Jesus."

Apparently he was originally called "Hoshea" (cf. Deut. 32:44), but later the abbreviation for the covenant name for Israel's deity, "YHWH," was prefixed.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:22 "the Lord your God is the one fighting for you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:22 "the Lord your God is the one fighting for you" This is not human effort, skills, or resources, but God's power (cf. Deut. 1:30; 20:4; Exod. 14:14; 15:3).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:23-29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:23-29 This is a very personal note from Moses. This is the only place in all the Bible that we have a recorded plea of Moses for himself. In other places he prayed for people or land. This is a glimpse into the heart of Moses, the man.

3:23
NASB, NKJV, NJB, JPSOA  "pleaded"
NRSV, LXX  "entreated"
TEV  "earnestly prayed"
Peshitta  "besought"

I earnestly implored (BDB 335, KB 334, Hithpael IMPERFECT with waw, cf. 1 Kgs. 8:33,47,59; 2 Chr. 6:37; Job 8:5; 9:15; Ps. 30:8; 142:1; Hosea 12:4) the Lord. Moses was in agony over not being allowed to enter the Promised Land.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:24 "O Lord God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:24 "O Lord God" The term for "Lord" here is the word adonai (lit. "my Lord," BDB 10; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD [adon and kurios]),which is the Hebrew word for "owner," "master," "husband," or "Lord."

The word "God" is the Hebrew word YHWH (BDB 217). He is saying literally "Lord, YHWH." This designation is seldom used in Moses' writings. This is Moses' prayer language.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "You have begun to show Your servant Your greatness and Your strong hand" Moses is pleading that his intimate knowledge of YHWH, His character (see full notes at Deut. 4:31 and 10:17), His acts should motivate YHWH to let him cross Jordan, but YHWH is no respecter of persons!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "for what god is there in heaven or earth who can do such works and mighty acts as Yours" Is this the concept that YHWH is the supreme God among many other spiritual beings, called henotheism (e.g. Exod. 15:11 and Deut. 4:7; 5:7)? Does this mean that

  1. Moses is affirming the existence of other gods (i.e. elohim)
  2. however, YHWH is the strongest
  3. Or is this monotheism (e.g. Deut. 4:35,39; 6:4; Exod. 20:2-3; Isa. 43:11; 44:6,8,24; 45:5,6-7,14,18,21,22), one and only one God?

We really do not know. I would rather believe that Moses is not referring to other gods, but to other spiritual forces, e.g. sometimes called elohim (cf. Ps. 8:5; 82:1,6; 1 Sam. 28:13; Ps. 89:5-8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS AND DEMONS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:25 "Let me, I pray, cross over and see"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:25 "Let me, I pray, cross over and see" This phrase has two VERBS:

  1. "cross over" ‒ BDB 716, KB 778, Qal COHORTATIVE
  2. "see" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERFECT, but in a COHORTATIVE sense

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:26 "the Lord was angry"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:26 "the Lord was angry" This is an example of anthropomorphic language ("angry" BDB 720, KB 780). How can we express God's being upset without using human terms? We can't, but we must remember that God is not a human and does not think and act like humans (i.e. Isa. 55:9-11). We use human terms to describe the nature of God knowing that fallen humans can not ultimately describe God.

Moses' public sin (cf. Deut. 32:51; Num. 20:10-12; 27:12-14) brought public consequences!

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (anthropomorphism)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

▣ "on your account" See notes at Deut. 1:34,37.

▣ "Enough! Speak to Me no more of this matter" Moses has been praying over and over (cf. Num. 20:2-13; 27:13; Deut. 1:37; 3:23-27), "I'm sorry, please let me go into the Promised Land." Finally YHWH said, "No, don't ask any more" (BDB 414, KB 418, Hiphil JUSSIVE).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:27 This verse and Deut. 3:28 have a series of commands in response to Moses' prayer:

  1. "go up" ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "lift up" ‒ BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "see" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. "charge" ‒ BDB 845, KB 1010, Piel IMPERATIVE
  5. "encourage" ‒ BDB 304, KB 302, Piel IMPERATIVE
  6. "strengthen" ‒ BDB 54, KB 65, Piel IMPERATIVE

YHWH made provision for Moses and for Israel (i.e. to empower Joshua, cf. Deut. 3:28b,c).

▣ "top of Pisgah" See note at Deut. 3:17.

▣ "lift up your eyes to the west and north and south and east, and see it with your eyes" This is a perfect example of God's love and His wrath. "I said you cannot go in, but I will let you see it."

▣ "for you shall not cross over this Jordan" God is not a respecter of persons. Moses was a great man of God, but he publicly disobeyed God and so he suffered the consequences (cf. Job 34:11; Ps. 28:4; 62:12; Prov. 24:12; Eccl. 12:14; Jer. 17:10; 32:19; Matt. 16:27; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:6; 14:12; 1 Cor. 3:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:7-10; 2 Tim. 4:14; 1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 2:23; 20:12; 22:12).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 3:29 "Beth-peor"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:29 "Beth-peor" This was literally "house/temple of Peor" (BDB 112). Peor was a mountain or city in northwest Moab. This was the site of Israel's idolatry (Ba'al fertility worship, cf. Numbers 22-23). It became part of the inheritance of Reuben (cf. Josh. 13:20).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What theological knowledge about God do we learn from this account?
  2. How do you relate the God of Deut. 3:3 and 6 to the God of the NT?
  3. Does Deut. 3:24 teach the existence of other gods?
  4. How did God show mercy and yet justice to Moses in Deut. 3:27?

entries.title: Deuteronomy 4:1 "listen"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:1 "listen" This VERB (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE) is used often in Deuteronomy (e.g. Deut. 1:16; 4:1; 5:1; 6:3,4; 9:1; 20:3; 27:10; 33:7). Its basic meaning is "to hear so as to do." It focuses on action, not just hearing (cf. James 1:22-25). This chapter has several warnings, Deut. 4:l, 2, 6, 9, 13, 14, 15, 19, 23, and 26 (cf. Micah 1:2; 3:1; 6:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

▣ "the statutes and the judgments" These include the collective revelations of God. It is all that God has revealed about Himself and His covenant requirements. It is similar in meaning to the word Torah (lit. "teachings," i.e. Mosaic legislation).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION (using DEUTERONOMY and PSALMS)

▣ "which I am teaching you" Moses served as YHWH's agent of deliverance and revelation (i.e. prophet, cf. Deut. 3:14; 4:1-17; 18:15-18; 34:10-12).

▣ "to perform" The INFINITIVE (BDB 793, KB 889, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) encourages the people to hear YHWH's law and then obey it (cf. Deut. 16:12; 30:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

▣ "so that they may go in and take possession of the land" Notice the conditional nature of YHWH's covenant (e.g. Deut. 5:33; 8:1; 16:20; 30:16,19). All of thee VERBS are Qal PERFECTS. The last VERB in Deut. 4:1 (giving) is a Qal PARTICIPLE. God's gift depends on Israel's actions!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: POSSESS THE LAND

▣ "the God of your fathers" This refers to the Patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, cf. Deut. 1:11,21; 4:1,31,37; 6:3; 12:1; 26:7; 27:3). All of the covenants with the Patriarchs involved conditions (except Genesis 6-9 and 15:12-21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS
