READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:2,7 "three cities"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:2,7 "three cities" These were Levitical cities of refuge, discussed in Numbers 35; Joshua 20, where someone accused of murder (i.e. "manslayer") could flee to protect himself from the dead person's relatives (i.e. "blood avenger"). The leaders of these cities were to hold a trial (cf. Deut. 19:11-13) to determine the facts of the case.

A list of the cites of refuge is found in Joshua 20:7-8:

  1.  Trans-jordan
    1.  Bezer in Reuben
    2.  Ramoth-Gilead in Gad
    3.  Golan in Manasseh (Bashan)
  2.  Canaan
    1.  Kadesh in Naphtali (Galilee)
    2.  Shechem in Ephraim
    3.  Hebron in Judah

The idea of a place of safety or refuge was not unique to Israel. Most Ancient Near Eastern and Mediterranean cultures provided these special places. Usually they were located at religious shrines. Israel also had this concept by one grabbing the "horns of the altar" at a local YHWH altar (cf. Exod. 27:2; 30:10; see Jewish Study Bible, p. 409) or at the central shrine (cf. Exod. 21:14; 1 Kgs. 1:50-53; 2:28-34). However, special cities of refuge were unique to Israel, although other ANE cultures had safe places, usually temples. YHWH was concerned with the death of innocent manslayers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CITIES OF REFUGE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:3 "prepare the roads"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:3 "prepare the roads" The VERB (BDB 465, KB 464, Hiphil IMPERFECT) here means "prepare a road." There are three possible meanings:

  1.  equal distance apart
  2.  easy access
  3.  "provide road signs pointing the way" (Rashi quoting a Maccabean document)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:4 "case of the manslayer"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:4 "case of the manslayer" This is an expansion of Exod. 21:12-14, which relates to the central sanctuary. This expanded the safety of the central sanctuary to the six Levitical cities of refuge.

▣ "who may flee there and live" If the one who killed someone fled (BDB 630, KB 681, Qal IMPERFECT) to one of the designated cities and if the ensuing trial found that there was no premeditation then he must live (BDB 310, KB 309, Qal PERFECT with waw) in that city of safety until the death of the current High Priest (cf. Josh. 20:6). Notice, there are consequences!

▣ "unintentionally" See note at Deut. 4:42. This is the opposite of "premeditated act."

SPECIAL TOPIC: UNINTENTIONAL SINS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:6 "avenger of blood"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:6 "avenger of blood" The phrase is a CONSTRUCT (BDB 145 I, KB 169, Qal PARTICIPLE and BDB 196, cf. Num. 35:9-28). This person is also known as "kinsman redeemer"(one who acts on behalf of the family). This is an example of Deut. 19:21's limited revenge (cf. Exod. 21:23-25; Lev. 24:19-22).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BLOOD AVENGER

▣ "though he was not deserving of death" This is a theological development of Gen. 9:5-6. Here the motive behind the action is taken into consideration. That which was accidental and unpremeditated is reprieved from "eye-for-an-eye" retaliation. There were consequences (had to live in the city of refuge until the death of the current High Priest).

Israel, like YHWH, was to be concerned with justice and limited revenge!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CITIES OF REFUGE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 19:7 Moses gave them YHWH's word in Deut. 19:1-3; he explained them in Deut. 19:4-6 and, then he reasserts YHWH's command in Deut. 19:7.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:8 "If"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:8 "If" The hypothetical PARTICLE (BDB 49) expresses the conditional nature of YHWH's covenant with Israel (cf. Deut. 19:9). He had given them the trans-Jordan area and now if they obeyed He would give them Canaan.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:9 "carefully observe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:9 "carefully observe" There is one VERB "to observe" (BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal IMPERFECT, see note at Deut. 6:12) followed by several INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS constructs:

  1.  "to do" ‒ BDB 793, KB 889
  2.  "to love" ‒ BDB 12, KB 17
  3.  "to walk" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, cf. Deut. 10:12; 11:1,13,22; 30:16

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

▣ "all this commandment" This SINGULAR term (BDB 846) is used to describe all of YHWH's covenant (cf. Deut. 4:2; 6:1; 11:8; 15:5; 19:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION, II. E.

▣ "you shall add three more cities" These three plus the three of Deut. 19:2 show the six cities of refuge mentioned in Joshua 20. These refer to

  1. the future three cities on the western side of the Jordan, not yet conquered
  2. Israel's later expansion of the text after Joshua's conquest (editorial update)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CITIES OF REFUGE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 19:10 YHWH is concerned about the death of people who do not deserve to die (i.e. "innocent blood," cf. 2 Kgs. 21:16; 24:4; Jer. 22:17). In the OT there is no distinction between ethical and ritual purity. Life is precious! Its loss has consequences ("blood-guiltiness," cf. Num. 35:33-34). It is this consequence and other ritual uncleanness that is dealt with (1) annually by the Day of Atonement, described in Leviticus 16, which dealt with the corporate sins of Israel and (2) locally by the sacrifice of a heifer (cf. Deut. 21:1-9). As the cities of refuge dwelt with individuals, Deut. 21:1-9 deals with the ritual guiltiness of communities.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:11 Notice the series of VERBS describing the premeditated murder:

  1.  "hates" ‒ BDB 971, KB 1338, Qal PARTICIPLE, cf. Deut. 4:42
  2.  "lies in wait" ‒ BDB 70, KB 83, Qal PERFECT with waw
  3.  "rises up" ‒ BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal PERFECT with waw
  4.  "strikes" ‒ BDB 645, KB 697, Qal PERFECT with waw

SPECIAL TOPIC: MURDER

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:12 "the elders of his city"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:12 "the elders of his city" This refers to either the city nearest the crime or the city of the man's residence.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELDER

▣ "the avenger of blood" See SPECIAL TOPIC: BLOOD AVENGER and SPECIAL TOPIC: "EYE FOR EYE" RETALIATION

▣ "that he may die" The taking of someone's life by the community was meant to be a deterrent to further crimes against the community citizens (cf. Deut. 13:11). In the OT the death sentence was carried out by the whole community (i.e. Lev. 20:2,27; 24:13-23; Num. 15:32-36; Deut. 13:10; 21:21; Josh. 7:22-26).

Here is a list of the sins that triggered capital punishment in Israel.

  1. all of the sins listed in Exod. 20:13-16 required capital punishment.
    1. murder
    2. adultery
    3. stealing (i.e. kidnapping, cf. Exod. 21:16; Deut. 24:7)
    4. false witnessing
  2. idolatry/occult
    1. Molelch ‒ Lev. 20:2-5; 1 Kgs. 11:7
    2. mediums and spiritists ‒ Lev. 20:6-8,27
    3. go after other gods ‒ Deut. 13:1-10; 17:2-7
  3. incest ‒ Lev. 20:14
  4. blasphemy against YHWH ‒ Exod. 22:28; Lev. 24:10-23
  5. sabbath breaking ‒ Num. 15:35-36
  6. premeditated murder ‒ Exod. 20:13; Num. 35:9
  7. dishonoring parents ‒ Exod. 21:17; Lev. 20:9; Deut. 21:18-21
  8. adultery ‒ Exod. 20:10-16; Deut. 22:13-21,22,23-27
  9. violating the ban (herem) ‒ Josh. 7:25

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:13 "You shall not pity him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:13 "You shall not pity him" This (BDB 299, KB 298, Qal IMPERFECT) is a recurrent theme in Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 7:16; 13:8; 19:13,21; 25:12). Human compassion or national feelings cannot change YHWH's laws. Israel must be holy! Israel's future prosperity (and even her remaining in the Promised Land) is conditioned on her obedience.

▣
NASB  "you shall purge the blood of the innocent
  from Israel"
NKJV  "you shall put away the guilt of innocent
  blood from Israel "
NRSV, Peshitta  "you shall purge the guilt of innocent blood
  from Israel"
TEV  "Israel must rid itself of murders"
NJB  "You must banish the shedding of innocent
  blood from Israel"

The VERB (BDB 128, KB 145, Piel PERFECT with waw) means "burn," used as imagery here of the complete removal of guilt from the nation (cf. Deut. 13:8; 17:7,12; 19:13,19; 21:21; 22:21,22,24; 24:7).

Murder affects individuals (cf. Genesis 4) and communities (cf. Deut. 21:1-9). Sin and self destroy everything they touch!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:14 "you shall not move your neighbor's boundary mark"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:14 "you shall not move your neighbor's boundary mark" In the ancient world villages farmed the land together (i.e. plowing, sowing, reaping). From a passerby's observation it looked like one big field. However, each family had its own field, which was marked by white stones. That family, though working the entire field with the village, received the produce of their land. If someone moved the stones, thereby giving themselves more land (i.e. produce), it was a crime against the whole community and YHWH, because He gave the land as an inheritance for each tribe and family in Joshua 13-19 (cf. Deut. 27:17; Prov. 22:28; 23:10; Hosea 5:10).

An example of this community farming concept is seen in the parable of Jesus in Matt. 13:1-23; Mark 4:1-20.

▣ "which the ancestors have set" This is the kind of statement that has caused many scholars to reject Mosaic authorship of Deuteronomy. It seems to refer to the allocation of land by lot, which occurred after Joshua's conquest (cf. Joshua 13-19). Egyptian scribes updated their texts, while Mesopotamian scribes did not. Israel's scribes were trained in Egypt.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCRIBES

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:15 This verse shows how careful they were to be in their judicial process (cf. Deut. 17:6; Num. 35:30). The VERB "rise up" (BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERFECT) is used three times in the Hebrew text of Deut. 19:15 and 16.

The Hebrew text has three "any's" (BD 481) which was a way to highlight the need for 2 or 3 witnesses to convict of "any" crimes (not just capital offenses; Deut. 17:6). The charged person was to be given the benefit of being considered innocence!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:16 "malicious witness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:16 "malicious witness" The NOUN "malicious" (BDB 329) basically means "violence," but here it denotes a purposeful, false judicial witness (cf. Exod. 23:1; Ps. 27:12; 35:11). They speak in YHWH's name (legal oath), but knowingly distort the truth. Verse 19 shows the consequences of a false witness (cf. Deut. 5:20 and chapter 11).

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV   "wrongdoing"
TEV   "false accusations"
NJB   "a charge of apostasy"
REB   "a crime"
LXX   "impiety"
JPSOA   "false testimony"

The Hebrew term (BDB 694 II) usually means "a rebellious attitude which becomes an action" (cf. Deut. 13:5; Jer. 28:16; 29:32). Here the context implies purposeful, premeditated "lying," which in Israel's legal system often resulted in the death penalty, so this is premeditated murder.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MURDER

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:17 "the priests and the judges"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:17 "the priests and the judges" This refers to:

  1.  local judges, Deut. 16:18-20; 17:8-13
  2.  Levitical priests of the central sanctuary, Deut. 18:1-8

Notice that appearing before these appointed judges is the same as appearing before YHWH (cf. Deut. 17:9,12).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:18 "The judges shall investigate thoroughly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 19:18 "The judges shall investigate thoroughly" See note at Deut. 13:15. This same word (BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE) is also used in Deut. 17:4.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:19 "you shall do to him just as he had intended to do to his brother"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 19:19 "you shall do to him just as he had intended to do to his brother" This is an example of "we reap what we sow" (see full list of texts at Jer. 17:10) or "an eye-for-an-eye" justice (cf. Lev. 24:19).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:20 "The rest will hear and be afraid"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 19:20 "The rest will hear and be afraid" There is a social deterrent in individual punishment by the community (cf. Deut. 13:11; 17:13). This is the rationale of the modern "death penalty."

entries.title: Deuteronomy 19:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:21 The "eye-for-an-eye" justice of Israel (i.e. Lev. 24:20), which seems so cruel (i.e. Lex talionis, which is also characteristic of the Code of Hammurabi, see Old Testament Times, by R. K. Harrison, pp. 57-61) was in reality meant to stop "revenge wars" between families and tribes (see SPECIAL TOPIC: BLOOD AVENGER) as well as maintain the ritual purity of God's covenant people.

One wonders about how literally this law was actually carried out. It seems that physical mutilation was replaced by appropriate compensation. This is based on the surrounding context of the parallel in Exod. 21:23-25. The immediately preceding and following contexts deal with compensation. The later rabbis assigned appropriate compensation for actions resulting in personal damage. However, murder retained its religious taboo. It negatively impacted the covenant of blessings from YHWH and had to be dealt with appropriately!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1.  Why did God establish cities of refuge?
  2.  Explain the concept of "the avenger of blood."
  3.  How did the Hebrews handle perjury?
  4.  What was the purpose of "eye-for-eye" justice?

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:1 "When you go out to battle. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:1 "When you go out to battle. . ." Notice the theological tension between

  1.  Israel preparing for battle
  2.  YHWH giving the victory

This involved human will and divine sovereignty. This is the covenant tension! YHWH demands a faith response!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION

▣ "horses and chariots" The Canaanites had many horses and chariots (i.e. the ultimate military weapon of that time and place); the Israelis had none (cf. Josh. 11:4; 17:16; Isa. 31:1-3; Hosea 14:3). The Israelites must trust in YHWH to provide the victory, not better weaponry (cf. Isa. 30:15-17; 31:1-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS

▣ "do not be afraid of them" This VERB (BDB 431, KB 4387, Qal IMPERFECT) is a recurrent theme in holy war contexts (cf. Deut. 1:21,29; 3:2,22; 7:18; 20:1,3; 31:6,8). They were not to fear the power or number of their Canaanite enemies, but they were to fear YHWH (cf. Deut. 4:10; 5:29; 6:2,13,24; 10:12,20; 13:4; 14:23; 17:19; 28:58; 31:12,13), because He is an awesome God (same Hebrew term, cf. Deut. 7:21; 10:17; 28:58).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

▣ "for the Lord your God, who brought you up from the land of Egypt" See Exod. 14:26-28 for a reference to YHWH's deliverance of His people from Pharaoh. Israel's trust was based on:

  1.  previous revelation to the Patriarchs
  2.  miraculous Egyptian deliverance
  3.  miraculous wilderness wandering provisions
  4.  victories on the eastern bank of Jordan

20:19-20 20:19-20 20:19-20 20:19-20

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1.  Deuteronomy 20 is a description of how Israel was to conduct "holy war," which is a war done in the name of YHWH, commanded by YHWH, and the rules of engagement controlled by YHWH, for the glory of YHWH (cf. Deut. 20:1-20; 21:10-14; 23:9-14; 24:5; 25:17-19).

  2.  The problem moderns have with this type of text usually involve an ethical outrage. However, it is just not fair to apply modern notions of ethics and warfare to ancient military practices.

    Another issue is the problem of modern Christians trying to apply every OT text to their day. It is not God's will that every generation in every locality reproduce an ancient Near Eastern culture, but that we seek the eternal truths bound up in the cultural actions, then apply these universal truths to our culture. A good book at this point is How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth by Fee and Stuart or Gospel and Spirit by Gordon Fee.

    Because it happened and is recorded in the Bible does not automatically mean it is God's will for every age and every culture (e.g. food laws, holy war, polygamy, slavery, subjection of women, etc.).

  3.  This chapter is a mixture of compassion and severity!

  4.  For a good brief discussion see Roland de Vaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, pp. 258-267.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:2 "the priest shall come near and speak to the people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 20:2 "the priest shall come near and speak to the people" The rabbis called this person "the anointed priest of battle." Before battle, the priest admonished them to be brave because God was with them. Even if some died in battle, God would still take care of all the soldiers and their families.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:3-4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:3-4 Notice the series of admonitions ("hear" BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE) of the priest in verse 3:

  1.  "do not be fainthearted" ‒ BDB 939, KB 1236, Qal IMPERFECT, but JUSSIVE in meaning, cf. Isa. 7:4; Jer. 51:46
  2.  "do not be afraid" ‒ BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT, but JUSSIVE in meaning, see note at Deut. 20:1
  3.  "do not panic" ‒ BDB 342, KB 339, Qal IMPERFECT, but JUSSIVE in meaning, cf Job 40:23 (examples: 1 Sam. 23:26; 2 Kgs. 7:15; Ps. 48:5)
  4.  "do not tremble before them" ‒ BDB 791, KB 888, Qal IMPERFECT, but JUSSIVE in meaning, cf. Deut. 1:29; 7:21; 31:6; Josh. 1:9

 The reason for the confidence is stated in Deut. 20:4:

  1.  "the Lord your God is the one who goes with you" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  2.  "to fight for you" ‒ BDB 535, KB 526, Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  3.  "to save you" ‒ BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:5-8 "The officers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:5-8 "The officers" This is a special Hebrew word (BDB 1009) sometimes used in conjunction with the local judges or military leaders. It means "the representatives from each tribe" (cf. Deut. 1:15; 29:10; 31:28).

The officers made the judgment on any exemptions to military service.

Here is a list of exemptions that allowed an Israelite man to not go into battle:

  1. One who built a new house and had not dedicated it, Deut. 20:5 (obviously a future event; there is no record of the nature or purpose of this procedure recorded in the OT, but the term is the same as the one used for dedicating the temple, BDB 335 II).
  2. One who has planted a vineyard and has not begun to use its fruit, Deut. 20:6 (obviously a future event, a vineyard took three years to produce fruit, cf. Lev. 19:23-25 for theological issues).
  3. One who is engaged, but has not married yet, Deut. 20:7, cf. Deut. 24:5.
  4. One who is afraid or fainthearted, Deut. 20:8, because it may cause others to be afraid, cf. Jdg. 7:3; I Macc. 3:56.

Numbers 1, 2, and 3 are related to inheritance issues. But they may also be seen in light of Deut. 28:30. These very things are mentioned as being results of covenant disobedience.

▣ "Let him depart and return to his house" This phrase is made up of the VERBS:

  1.  "depart" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERFECT used as a JUSSIVE
  2.  "return" ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal JUSSIVE

It is repeated with each possible exemption listed (cf. Deut. 20:5,6,7,8). It was not the size of Israel's army, but the power of Israel's God that made the difference! The smaller and less equipped the army, the more it magnified God's victory (cf. Judges 7).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:10-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 20:10-15 These are surrender instructions about distant cities, cities on the periphery or out of the bounds of the Promised Land that God gave (i.e. outside Israel's inheritance, cf. Deut. 20:15).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:11 "shall become your forced labor and shall serve you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 20:11 "shall become your forced labor and shall serve you" This reflects a common element of ancient Near Eastern warfare.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:13 "the edge of the sword"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 20:13 "the edge of the sword" The literal Hebrew is "to the mouth of the sword" (BDB 804 CONSTRUCT BDB 352). The implication is that all the men of a certain age were killed.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:14 In the ancient world soldiers were not paid a salary, but their compensation was the spoils of victory. In Israel, especially "holy war," the spoils belonged to YHWH to show that the victory was His victory and that the land was His land. These verses are exceptions because these cities were outside the Promised Land.

▣ "the women" Even captured slaves had some rights (cf. Deut. 21:10-14), which shows YHWH's compassion for non-Israelites.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:16 "you shall not leave alive anything that breathes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 20:16 "you shall not leave alive anything that breathes" This means small children, pregnant women, old people, animals. . .anything that breathes (cf. Josh. 10:40; 11:11,14).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:16-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:16-18 These verses refer to cities within the Promised Land. These cities are totally under the ban of destruction (cf. Deut. 20:16-17).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEREM

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:17 "utterly destroy"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:17 "utterly destroy" The word here is herem (BDB 355, KB 353 I, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Hiphil IMPERFECT of the same root, which was a grammatical way to show intensity), which is the idea of total and complete destruction because it has been dedicated to God (cf. Deut. 2:34; 7:1-5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: UTTERLY DESTROY

▣ "the Hittite and the Amorite, the Canaanite and the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:18 How can this be done by a loving God? One answer is found in Deut. 20:18 - a theological reason. If you don't wipe them out they will theologically pollute you. Another answer is found in Deut. 9:4 and a third in Gen. 15:12-21. Human sins have consequences!

▣ "detestable things" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATIONS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 20:19-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:19-20 Walled cities in the ancient Near East were attacked by wooden siege machines. The wood was to be taken from non-fruit bearing tree, probably because this produce would be needed later by the Israeli inhabitants of the defeated city.

20:19
NASB, NJB  "is the tree of the field a man"
NKJV  "for the tree of the field is man's food"
NRSV, JPSOA, LXX  "are trees in the field human beings"
TEV  "the trees are not your enemy"

The Hebrew text is difficult here. It seems to mean that the trees are not the enemy! They were YHWH's way of providing immediate and future food for His people.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1.  How was Israel's fear of greater numbers and technology dealt with?
  2.  List the four exemptions from military service.
  3.  Did God advocate slavery (Deut. 20:11)?
  4.  How can one reconcile Deut. 20:16-17 with our view of God?
  5.  List all the humanitarian aspects of this chapter.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1.  Notice the recurrent pattern of "if. . .then." This is one type of ancient Near Eastern law (i.e. case law or casuistic law), which is distinct from apodictic law (e.g. the Ten Words/Ten Commandments).
    SPECIAL TOPIC: LAWS OF THE ANE

  2.  Deuteronomy's law code has several unique features:
    1.  recurrent emphases on covenant love
      1.  YHWH to Israel
      2.  Israelite to Israelite
      3.  Israelite to foreigner
      4.  Israelite to animals
    2. special care for the poor, disenfranchised, and powerless

  3.  YHWH instructs His people in clear ways (paths). He wants them to understand and act appropriately. Their actions are to reflect His character as a means of reaching those who do not yet know Him (personal and national faith relationship). The Law is God's gift to fallen humanity, not a capricious exercise of control! They show in many practical and specific ways how an "unholy people" can stay in fellowship with holy God!
    SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WAY. . .THE PATH

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:1-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:1-9 This is a context about how to cleanse the land when a murdered person is found in an open field, away from any city. Murder pollutes YHWH's land (e.g. Deut. 7:13; 11:9,21; 28:11; 30:20) and must be dealt with in an appropriate manner (i.e. sacrifice).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:2 "elders and judges"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:2 "elders and judges" There are local appointed leaders who sat in the gates of the city and tried the cases of the community. Only if they had a problem did they take the cases to a higher authority (i.e. Levitical priests, cf. Deut. 21:5). They measured the distance from the found body to the cities around. The nearest town had to perform certain rituals (cf. Deut. 21:3-8). This demonstrates their sense of guilt by proximity. The closest city was responsible for the blood-guiltiness, which could affect YHWH's blessings on the whole region (cf. Deut. 19:13).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:3 "heifer. . .which has not been worked and which has not pulled in a yoke"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:3 "heifer. . .which has not been worked and which has not pulled in a yoke" This means a heifer which has not been used for agricultural work.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:4 "a valley with running water which has not been plowed or sown"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:4 "a valley with running water which has not been plowed or sown" The valley, too, had to be in a natural state with running water (i.e. not a wadi). The water symbolized carrying the guilt away (similar to the goat of Leviticus 16).

▣ "shall break the heifer's neck" Later rabbinical Midrash said "chopped head off with an ax" because breaking the neck was a difficult task (cf. Exod. 13:13; 34:20). However, blood does not seem to be involved in the ritual, but the concept of substitution. The innocent heifer ceremonially takes the place of the unknown murderer. The purpose was to rid the land of bloodguiltiness (cf. Num. 35:33-34).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:5 "the priests"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:5 "the priests" They may refer later to local Levites. In Deuteronomy there is no distinction between priests and Levites (cf. Deut. 18:1-8).

▣ "to bless in the name of the Lord" Blessing was one of the functions of priests/Levites (cf. Deut. 10:8; 1 Chr. 23:13). One example of a priestly blessing is recorded in Num. 6:22-26. This blessing is related to Israel's covenant keeping (cf. Num. 6:27; Deut. 28:3-6). YHWH's personal presence (i.e. name) was honored or rejected by each Israelite's obedience or willful disobedience to YHWH's revelation (i.e. covenant). Israel's blessing, both individual (cf. Exod. 19:5-6) and corporate, was determined not by arbitrary or capricious choice, but by personal faith in YHWH, demonstrated by covenant obedience (lifestyle). YHWH wanted to bless (cf. Exod. 20:24; 2 Chr. 30:27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH

▣ "every dispute and every assault shall be settled by them" The VERB is the common one, "to be" (BDB 224, KB 243, Qal IMPERFECT). The translation "be settled" comes from the previous NOUN phrase, "by their word" (BDB 804).

There are two types of legal problems mentioned:

  1.  "dispute" (i.e. lawsuit) ‒ BDB 936, cf. Deut. 1:12; 19:17; 21:5; 25:1; Exod. 23:2,3,6
  2.  "assault" ‒ BDB 619, cf. Deut. 17:8. Here it refers to physical attack, but the term can mean disease, cf. Deut. 24:8 (many times in Leviticus).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:6 "wash their hands over the heifer"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:6 "wash their hands over the heifer" This symbolizes cleansing (cf. Ps. 26:6; 73:13) from guilt by the proximity of the dead body. The elders represent the whole community as they corporately wash the guilt away from the village and area.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:7 "Our hands did not shed this blood nor did our eyes see it"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:7 "Our hands did not shed this blood nor did our eyes see it" The rabbinical Midrash relates this to help for the stranger, poor, orphan, or widow. Since the villagers did not see the stranger's need for help they were absolved from meeting that need. This may have been a way to stop the victim's family (i.e. blood avenger) from killing an innocent member of the nearest village in retaliation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BLOOD AVENGER

21:8
NASB, TEV, NJB  "Forgive"
NKJV  "Provide atonement"
NRSV, JPSOA  "Absolve"
REB  "accept expiation"
LXX  "Be merciful"
Peshitta  "Pardon"

This is the Hebrew VERB "cover" ( BDB 497, KB 493, Piel IMPERATIVE). It is used twice in this verse (the second use is a Hithpael PERFECT with waw). This term, so common in Leviticus and Numbers, is used only three times in Deuteronomy: Deut. 21:8 [twice] and Deut. 32:43). Its basic meaning is "to ritually cover by means of a sacrifice."

SPECIAL TOPIC: ATONEMENT

▣ "redeemed" This VERB (BDB 804, KB 911, Qal PERFECT, but JUSSIVE in meaning) is parallel to "forgive" (i.e. cover).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RANSOM/REDEEM

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORGIVENESS IN THE OT

▣
NASB  "do not place the guilt of innocent blood in the
  midst of Your people"
NKJV  "do not lay innocent blood to the charge of Your
  people"
NRSV, JPSOA  "do not let the guilt of innocent blood remain in
  the midst of your people"
TEV  "do not hold us responsible for the murder of an
  innocent person"
NJB  "let no innocent blood be shed among your people"

The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERFECT, but in a JUSSIVE sense) is a prayer for ritual absolution from the consequences of an unsolved murder. Notice how NJB translates the phrase as a JUSSIVE.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:9 The ritual (cf. Deut. 21:1-8) was seen as "purging" (BDB 128, KB 145, Piel IMPERFECT) the effects of corporate sin (i.e. unsolved murders) from the whole community (similar to the rituals of "the Day of Atonement" in Leviticus 26). Sin, even unintentional corporate sin, affects the blessing of YHWH and even brings collective wrath (i.e. curses, cf. Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:10-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:10-14 These verses address how to appropriately deal with women (i.e. not Canaanites, but others, cf. Deut. 20:10-15) captured in war, even they had rights in YHWH's land. This care for the poor, powerless, and women is unique in the ancient world's law codes.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:11 "woman"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:11 "woman" This was not a Canaanite woman, a foreigner, but not Canaanite, living in the Promised Land.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

▣ Notice the verbal progression:

  1.  "see" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal PERFECT with waw
  2.  "love" ‒ BDB 365 I, KB 362, Qal PERFECT with waw, used of YHWH's love for Israel in Deut. 7:7; 10:15
  3.  "take" ‒ BDB 542, KB 534, Qal PERFECT with waw. Here it does not imply a sexual union, but a taking into one's house (cf. Deut. 21:12).

This same sequence is found in Gen. 3:6!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:12 "she shall shave her head and trim her nails"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:12 "she shall shave her head and trim her nails" This was a

  1.  concluding act (cf. Num. 6:9,18-19)
  2.  cleansing act (cf. Lev. 13:33; 14:8-9)
  3.  mourning act (cf. Deut. 14:1; Lev. 21:5; Jer. 41:5; Ezek. 44:20) ritual

Here it symbolized a new day, a new life, a new family. It is interesting that her conversion to YHWH is assumed, but not stated. The husband's faith was the family's faith!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOUSEHOLD BAPTISMS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:13 "and mourn her father and mother"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:13 "and mourn her father and mother" Although the text does not specifically state that this woman must be unmarried, it is implied. There is no mention of mourning over the loss of a husband nor the mention of children.

▣ "after that you may go in to her" This is a Hebrew idiom for sexual intercourse (i.e. which consummated the marriage). Notice that a desire for sexual relations, even with a non-Israelite, is not condemned, but there is an appropriate time. This month of mourning gives the Hebrew man time to get to know his potential wife. If things do not go well, there is a way out without divorce.

Also note the apparent absence of an actual marriage ceremony (cf. Gen. 24:67).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:14 "let her go"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:14 "let her go" This is the technical word for divorce (BDB 1018, KB 1511, Piel PERFECT with waw). She could not be sold (Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal IMPERFECT of BDB 569, KB 5181, which was a grammatical way to express emphasis) like a slave, but she could be divorced. See note at Deut. 24:1-4.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CERTIFICATE OF DIVORCE

▣
NASB  "you shall not mistreat her"
NKJV  "you shall not treat her brutally"
NRSV, TEV  "you must not treat her as a slave"
NJB  "you must not make any profit out of her"
JPSOA  "you must not enslave her"
REB  "treat her harshly"
LXX  "you shall not break faith with her"
Peshitta  "you shall not make a harlot of her"

The VERB (BDB 771 II, KB 849, Hithpael IMPERFECT) means "deal tyrannically with" or "forced to submit to the will of a more powerful person" (cf. Deut. 24:7). YHWH cares for the fair treatment of even captured women!

▣
NASB, NKJV, LXX, Peshitta  "because you have humbled
  her"
NRSV  "since you have dishonored
  her"
TEV  "since you forced her to have
  intercourse with you"
NJB  "since you have exploited her"
REB, JPSOA  "since you have had your will
  with her"

This VERB (BDB 776, KB 853, Piel PERFECT), in this context, is best translated like the TEV (e.g. Gen. 34:2; Deut. 22:24,29; Jdg. 19:24; 20:5; 2 Sam. 13:12,14,22,32). These women would have suffered:

  1.  capture in war
  2.  loss of family
  3.  forced integration into marriage, which also assumes a religious conversion
  4.  now forced removal from the home with no place to go

Notice that this paragraph, and the next also, limits the cultural power of male Israelites!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:15 This paragraph recognizes the cultural practice of polygamy. The first example in the OT is Lamech (Gen. 4:23). The most famous early polygamist was Jacob in Genesis 29. Polygamy was practiced in the ANE among wealthy or powerful people, not usually the common people (although Deut. 21:10-14 could refer to bigamy).

The exact motive for the practice is uncertain:

  1.  sexual
  2.  reproductive (an heir)
  3.  economic
    1.  help poor family
    2.  a way to gain wealth and influence
    3.  a way to handle the spoils of war
  4.  political unions to help neighboring nations maintain peace (i.e. David, Solomon)

▣ "unloved" As verses 10-14 dealt with captured women, verses 15-17 deal with the less favored wife. This is literally "hated" (BDB 971, cf. Deut. 21:15[twice],16,17). But it is functioning here as a Hebrew idiom of comparison—loved versus unloved (cf. Gen. 29:30-31; Mal. 1:2-3; Rom. 9:13 [quotes Mal. 1:2-3]; Luke 14:26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HATE

▣ "firstborn son" The firstborn's rights were established even if he were the son of the unloved wife (cf. Deut. 21:17; Exod. 13:14-15; Lev. 3:12-13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRSTBORN

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:17 "double portion"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:17 "double portion" The Hebrew idiom (BDB 804, "mouth" CONSTRUCT BDB 1040, "double") is also used of Elisha's desire related to Elijah in 2 Kgs. 2:9. This is the only place in the OT that this double portion is specifically mentioned. If there were two sons, the older would receive two-thirds and the younger one-third; if three sons, then 50%, 25%, 25%, etc. The oldest son was to care for the aged parents and administer the family assets.

It is interesting that the historicity of these laws is demonstrated by the archaeological finds of other ancient law codes:

  1.  Jacob in Genesis 49 gives all his twelve sons equal inheritance. This is reflected in the Code of Hammurabi
  2.  Here the mention of a double share for the firstborn is paralleled in the Nuzi and Mari tablets.
  3.  The differences recorded in Scripture reflect the differences in their contemporary culture (see The Old Testament Documents by Walter C. Kaiser, Jr., p. 86).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:18 This type of antisocial youth was characterized as:

  1. "stubborn" ‒ BDB 710, KB 770, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  2. "rebellious" ‒ BDB 598, KB 632, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  3. both of these things are used together in Ps. 78:8 and Jer. 5:23

The five PARTICIPLES in this verse show continuous action. The rest of the verse describes their actions:

  1. who will not obey parents, Deut. 21:18,20
  2. he will not even listen to them, Deut. 21:18
  3. glutton, Deut. 21:20 ‒ BDB 272 II
  4. drunkard, Deut. 21:20 ‒ BDB 684

See Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp.174-175.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:18-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:18-21 This section deals with rebellious sons (i.e. those who did not honor their parents, cf. Deut. 5:16) and how parents were to treat them (cf. Exod. 21:15,17; Lev. 20:9). Parents did not have the right of life or death over a child, but the courts did. This concerned

  1. the violation of Deut. 5:16
  2. the inheritance within a family
  3. community solidarity

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:19 "father and mother shall seize him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:19 "father and mother shall seize him" This means either

  1. both parents mutually restrain (BDB 1074, KB 1779, Qal PERFECT with waw)
  2. the need for two witnesses (cf. Deut. 17:6; 19:15; Num. 35:10)

▣ "at the gateway" The local place of justice was the city gate, where the elders sat (e.g. Deut. 19:12; 22:15; 25:7).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:21 "all the men of his city shall stone him to death"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:21 "all the men of his city shall stone him to death" Notice the humanitarian aspect that the parents did not have to stone their own son. The community (cf. Lev. 20:2,27; 24:14-23; Num. 15:35) acted to rid itself of evil, willfully recalcitrant members.

Do you still want to take the OT literally in our day?

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEATH PENALTY IN ISRAEL

▣
NASB, LXX  "you shall remove"
NKJV, Peshitta  "you shall put away"
NRSV  "you shall purge"
TEV, REB  "you will get rid of"
NJB  "you must banish"
JSPOA  "you will sweep out"

The Hebrew VERB (BDB 128, KB 145, Piel PERFECT with waw) means to burn in the sense of utterly remove (cf. Deut. 13:5; 17:7,12; 19:13,19; 21:9,21; 22:21,22,24; 24:7).

▣ "and all Israel will hear of it and fear" Societal punishment functions as a deterrent. See note at Deut. 13:11.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:22 "you hang him on a tree"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:22 "you hang him on a tree" See SPECIAL TOPIC: HANG

entries.title: Deuteronomy 21:23 "you shall surely bury"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:23 "you shall surely bury" This intensified construction combines the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal IMPERFECT of "bury" (BDB 868, KB 1064) of the same root. YHWH's wrath demanded the offender's death as the penalty for his stubborn rebellion. However, YHWH's displeasure would transfer to the community if the body of the executed covenant violator was not dealt with properly and in a timely fashion.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

SPECIAL TOPIC: CREMATION

▣ "(for he who is hanged is accursed of God)" See Gal. 3:13 for Paul's use of this phrase. Paul saw the substitutionary death of Jesus as taking on Himself the curse of the Mosaic law (i.e. Gal. 3:13; Phil. 2:8). The Mosaic Law became a death sentence (cf. Ezek. 18:4,20). Originally this curse was related to proper burial procedures in the holy land (i.e. possibly impaling a corpse on a stake for a brief period of time).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CURSE (ANATHEMA)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S VIEWS OF THE MOSAIC LAW

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why were innocent town's people guilty for unknown murder?
  2. What is unusual about the heifer and its death?
  3. Why did the captured women shave their heads?
  4. List the privilege of the first-born.
  5. How does Deut. 21:23 differ from Jesus' death? How are they related?

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:1 "You shall not see. . .and pay no attention"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:1 "You shall not see. . .and pay no attention" Purposeful or apathetic neglect ("hide oneself," BDB 761, KB 834, Hithpael PERFECT with waw, cf. Deut. 22:1,3,4; Lev. 20:4; Prov. 28:27; Ezek. 22:26) of a needy covenant brother's property is prohibited (cf. Deut. 22:3; Exod. 23:4-5).

▣ "bring them back" This common VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil) is used three times in Deut. 22:1-2. Its basic meaning is "return" or "turn back." Israel was meant to function as a caring family unit. Paragraphs like this spell out what Lev. 19:18 means in practical, specific ways. Brothers look out for brothers!

This first usage is intensified by the use of the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the IMPERFECT VERB of the same root, "you shall certainly bring them back!" This same type of intensification is used in Deut. 22:4, "you shall certainly help him to raise them up" (i.e. INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of BDB 877, KB 1086).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:5 This verse has been proofed-texted to dictate appropriate dress for modern worship (i.e. women cannot wear slacks to church). It must be remembered that both male and female wore robes in the ANE. The only difference being that women's robes in Israel had blue decoration around the shoulders.

The basic thrust of this text is the rejection of Canaanite worship practices (i.e. "abomination," cf. Lev. 18:26,27,29,30). There is to be a appropriate distinction between the God-given difference between males and females (i.e. the created order). This is not meant to be a negative, restricting distinction, but an affirmation of the different strengths and cultural functions of the sexes! See note on "Transvestism in the ANE" in IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p.194

It is surely possible that this text is connected to the Mosaic covenant's condemnation of homosexuality (cf. Lev. 18:22; 20:13) practiced in worship settings by the Canaanites.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOMOSEXUALITY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:6-7 These verses seen to relate to the preservation of food sources through many generations of Israelites. After Genesis 3 humanity could eat meat, but they must guard against the destruction of the source of the meat for the benefit of future generations of covenant brothers (i.e. "that you may prolong your days," cf. Deut. 4:40). Wild animals were God's gift of protein for His people. Many of these specific detailed regulations were meant to cause Israelites to think about their covenant responsibility to love, protect, and provide for the health and growth of the covenant people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NATURAL RESOURCES

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:7 "you shall certainly let the mother go"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:7 "you shall certainly let the mother go" The same type of emphasis found in Deut. 22:1 and 4 (i.e. INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root, BDB 1018, KB 1511) is repeated.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:8 "parapet for your roof"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:8 "parapet for your roof" A parapet (BDB 785, which in Arabic means "hinder") was a protective barrier around the top of flat-roofed homes to keep people from falling. Again Israel was to think about how to protect covenant brothers, sisters, and family members!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:9 "You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:9 "You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed" This apparently does not specifically refer to the types of grapevines in a field, but it is assumed the principle would dictate only one type per vineyard. This refers to the seasonal crops sowed between the grapevines.

This may reflect (1) a Canaanite practice to appease the gods or (2) the mentality that mixing things causes the loss of purity (cf. Lev. 19:19).

▣ "defiled" Kadosh (BDB 872, KB 1073, Qal IMPERFECT) means set apart for God (cf. Deut. 15:19). This could mean (1) it had to be destroyed or (2) given to the priests. Does this principle apply today? I would assert that OT laws must be repeated in the NT to be binding on New Covenant believers (cf. Acts 15; 1 Corinthians 8-10; Galatians 3). Jesus, Himself negated both the sacrificial system and the food laws (cf. Mark 7:17-23). The whole structure of the NT book of Hebrews is the superiority of the NT over the OT. Two books that have helped me think through the issue are:

  1. How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth by Gordon Fee and Doug Stuart
  2. Gospel and Spirit by Gordon Fee

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT OVER THE MOSAIC COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSAIC LAW AND THE CHRISTIAN

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:10 "You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:10 "You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey" Oxen were clean, donkeys were unclean, but this prohibition, so said the rabbis, was done as a humanitarian gesture to animals of different strengths and characteristics. However, in context, it is just one more example of "do not mix things!"

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:11 "You shall not wear a material mixed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:11 "You shall not wear a material mixed" This is another exclusion of mixed things (cf. Lev. 19:19). It may have been imagery of mixing YHWHistic and Canaanite worship practices. Some even see it (1) connected to magic clothes (i.e. patterns of mixed materials) or (2) the Dead Sea Scrolls (i.e. 4QMMT) mentions that only certain types of clothing could be mixed (i.e. priestly garments were made from wool and linen, which would denote a sacred sense. Maybe that is why unsanctioned mixing was considered "defiled."

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:12 In this context this probably continues the rejection of anything Canaanite. Israel was to have different worship, different God, different dress! In Num. 15:37-42 these tassels have the added meaning of reminding the Israelites to keep and cherish the law. This same type of symbolism is reflected in the tallith (prayer shawl) of Jesus' day. The garment referred to was a rectangular cloth used to cover the upper part of the person, especially during worship, prayer, and reading Scripture. It is unsure if the tassels were also required (or allowed) on women's clothing. This may be another item related to cross-dressing (cf. Deut. 22:5).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:13 "goes in to her"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:13 "goes in to her" This is one of three euphemisms for sexual intercourse used in this context:

  1. "goes in to her," Deut. 22:13 (BDB 97)
  2. "when I came near her," Deut. 22:14 (BDB 897)
  3. "lying with," Deut. 22:22,23,25,28,29 (BDB 1011)

 There are several VERBS which denote sexual activity.

  1. lie with, BDB 1011, KB 1486, cf. Gen. 19:32; 26:10; 30:15; 39:7; Lev. 18:22
  2. approach, BDB 897, KB 1132, cf. Gen. 20:4; Lev. 18:6,14,19; 20:16
  3. go in to, BDB 97, KB 112, cf. Gen. 19:31; 29:21,23,30; 30:3,4,16; 38:8,9,16; 39:14
  4. know, BDB 393, KB 390, cf. Gen. 4:1,17,25; 19:5,8; 24:16; 38:26; Num. 31:17,18,35; Jdgs. 19:22,25; 21:12

▣ "turns against her" This is the Hebrew word "hates" (BDB 971, KB 1338). It is the same word used in Deut. 21:15, which is translated "unloved" and is a Hebrew idiom of comparison, which is the concept of "loved more," "preferred." However, here it takes on the meaning of "rejects" or "is not happy with."

SPECIAL TOPIC: HATE

22:14
NASB, NJB  "publicly defames her"
NKJV, REB, LXX, Peshitta  "brings a bad name on her"
NRSV  "slandering her"
TEV  "makes up false charges against
  her"

Literally this is "brings upon her an evil name" (VERB ‒ BDB 422, KB 425, Hiphil PERFECT with waw and NOUN ‒ BDB 1027, and ADJECTIVE ‒ BDB 948). This is similar to Deut. 24:1-4, where a certificate of divorce is issued for "some indecency," which is assumed to be sexual in nature. The accused woman has little or no recourse for the loss of her (and her family's) reputation. Her future marriage opportunities and the inheritance of her child (if one is conceived early) is at stake. This was a very serious issue to Near Eastern people!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CERTIFICATE OF DIVORCE

▣ "I did not find her a virgin" The Hebrew society put a premium on virginity (cf. Deut. 22:19). Inheritance was a very important gift from God. Promiscuity was aggressively condemned!

The VERB "find" (BDB 592, KB 619) is used several times in this context:

  1. to find, to discover
    1. legally, Deut. 22:14,17,20
    2. physically, Deut. 22:23,27,28
  2. to catch in an act, Deut. 22:22,23

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:15 "the girl's father and mother shall take and bring out the evidence"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:15 "the girl's father and mother shall take and bring out the evidence" This is either (1) the Deuteronomy concept of mutuality of the raising up of women to be included in the Law or (2) two witnesses being required.

▣ "the evidence of the girl's virginity" This (BDB 144) can refer to:

  1. the parents broke the hymen before they gave their daughter to be married and kept fluids on a garment
  2. the bed covering at the time of the initial consummation of the marriage was given to and kept by the parents
  3. evidence that the girl was regularly menstruating before the wedding to prove that she was not pregnant

Number 1 seems to be ruled out because the husband would not have known for sure when this was done.

▣ "elders of the city at the gate" This would refer to the appointed judges who held court at the city gate or at a designated place (i.e. large tree, unique landmark, or main road).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELDERS

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:18 "shall take the man and chastise him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:18 "shall take the man and chastise him" This may mean to beat the man with forty stripes (cf. Deut. 25:2-3), but if so it is the only usage of this term (BDB 415, KB 418) in the OT where it usually refers to instruction (cf. Deut. 21:18, NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 479-481).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:19 "fine him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:19 "fine him" The man was to be punished and fined because he had defamed (literally, "brought an evil name") a virgin of Israel. The fine was apparently double what he paid (dowry) for the girl as a bride (cf. Deut. 22:29). The implication may be that he simply wanted to get his money back from the girl's father.

▣ "a virgin of Israel" This (BDB 143) was an honorific (but expected) descriptive title of all brides-to-be in YHWH's theocracy.

SPECIAL TOPIC: VIRGIN

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:19, 29 "she shall remain his wife; he cannot divorce her all his day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:19, 29 "she shall remain his wife; he cannot divorce her all his day" This was a limit on the man's rights. Women in Israel had no right to divorce. This rule was protecting the woman's children's rights to inheritance (cf. Deut. 21:15-17).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CERTIFICATE OF DIVORCE

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:20, 21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:20, 21 Normally, stoning was done outside the gate of the city. Because of the Hebrew concept of corporality, the father was responsible for his daughter's actions and, therefore, the punishment occurred at his door!

The penalty for a false witness was usually death. A clear double standard is seen here where, if the husband's accusation is true the girl is stoned, but if it is false (even malicious) he is chastened and fined, but not stoned (cf. Deut. 19:19). Women did not have the same legal rights and protection as males in the OT. Compassion is shown, but no legal rights!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEATH PENALTY IN ISRAEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: STONE TO DEATH

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:21 "an act of folly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:21 "an act of folly" This term (BDB 615) is used of inappropriate sexual activity:

  1. Gen. 34:7 (non-Israelite forces himself on Jacob's daughter)
  2. Deut. 22:21 (loss of virginity)
  3. Jdg. 19:23; 20:6,10 (pagans attack a Levite's concubine)
  4. 2 Sam. 13:12-13 (Amnon, David's first son, rapes his half-sister)

▣ "playing the harlot" This term is the Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT of a term (BDB 275, KB 275) which denoted inappropriate sexual activity involving

  1. fornication (sex before marriage)
  2. adultery (sex after marriage with someone other then your spouse)
  3. prostitution (sex for hire)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ADULTERY

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:22 "If a man is found lying with a married woman"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:22 "If a man is found lying with a married woman" Even if there is suspicion there is recourse (cf. Num. 5:11-31).

The phrase "a married woman" is literally "the wife of another man," which is a double use of the term b'l (BDB 127, KB 142, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE and NOMINATIVE MASCULINE SINGULAR NOUN form). This term, normally translated "lord" or "husband," has the same root as Ba'al, the male Canaanite fertility god. The husband was "lord" over his home. His wife and children were, in a legal sense, property. In actuality sexual violations were seen as a sin against God (cf. Gen. 39:9; 2 Sam. 12:13). It violates the God-given order and stability of society and affects the God-given inheritance of families and clans.

▣ "both of them shall die" The later rabbis interpreted this to mean the child, too, if the woman was pregnant, because of the idea of corporate sin (Joshua 7). Notice the equality of the punishment (both man and woman), which is unusual in the OT.

The Mosaic legislation parallels the Code of Hammurabi at this point (see R. K. Harrison, OT Times, p. 59).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:23 "virgin"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:23 "virgin" See SPECIAL TOPIC: VIRGIN

▣ "engaged" In Israel being engaged (BDB 76, KB 91, Pual PARTICIPLE) was as legally binding as being married (i.e. Joseph and Mary, cf. Matt. 1:18-19).

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:24 "you shall stone them. . .because she did not cry out in the city"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:24 "you shall stone them. . .because she did not cry out in the city" Both would be stoned to death (cf. Lev. 20:10); the man because he violated a neighbor's wife, the woman because she did not cry out (BDB 858, KB 1042, Qal PERFECT) for help.

▣ "Thus you shall purge the evil from among you" See note at Deut. 13:5.

Because of the influence of Canaanite fertility worship, Israel must behave differently and appropriately with women in the home and society.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:25-27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:25-27 The legislation of Israel was meant to be fair, not just legalistic. There were innocent parties to sinful acts!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:28 "If a man finds a girl who is a virgin, who is not engaged, and seizes her and lies with her"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:28 "If a man finds a girl who is a virgin, who is not engaged, and seizes her and lies with her" Considering the early age at which Jewish girls were usually engaged, it seems to me this might be referring to (1) child abuse or (2) the abuse of poor families. The Mosaic covenant protects the under privileged and socially powerless!

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:29 "the man . . .shall give to the girl's father fifty shekels. . .cannot divorce her"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:29 "the man . . .shall give to the girl's father fifty shekels. . .cannot divorce her" If a father was too poor to have his daughter engaged or the girl was mentally incapacitated and a man defiled her, then he must pay for her and marry her for life (cf. Exod. 22:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES, II. A. 2.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 22:30 "A man shall not take his father's wife"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:30 "A man shall not take his father's wife" This probably means a man cannot marry his stepmother (possibly one of several wives), even if the father has died or the woman has been divorced.

▣ "his father's skirt" This is an idiomatic way of referring to the father's marital activities (cf. Ruth 3:9; Ezek. 16:8). To be intimate with a woman who had previously been intimate with one's father was, in a sense, a violation of the father (cf. Deut. 27:20; Lev. 18:8; 20:11).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. How much of this chapter would you say applies to our culture? How do you determine your decision?
  2. What is the background of these laws?

entries.title: Deuteronomy 23:1 "emasculated"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:1 "emasculated" This English word translated two Hebrew terms:

  1.  "by crushing" ‒ BDB 194
  2.  "to wound or bruise" ‒ BDB 822, KB 954, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE

This refers to (1) a male's testicles being removed or (2) the severing of the spermatic cord (possibly by crushing).

▣ "or has his male organ cut off" This refers to a severed penis (BDB 1050, "a place of pouring fluid"). This would be another way of describing a eunuch (cf. Matt. 19:12). These two damaged males are the first in a series of those who are excluded from attendance at the assemblies of Israel (i.e. events at the tabernacle). Their exclusion is symbolic of the purity and wholeness of God's people seen as a kingdom of priests (cf. Exod. 19:6 and Lev. 21:17-23; 22:17-25). Later in the OT many of these excluded ones are included (e.g. Ruth the Moabitess and the eunuch of Isa. 56:3-5 and Acts 8:26-40).

It is also possible that this practice of damaging a male's sexual potential was part of Canaanite practices. Many of the seemingly unusual prohibitions in the Mosaic legislation were directed at a total break with Canaanite society and worship practices.

▣ "shall enter" This VERB (BDB 97, KB 112) is used several times in this chapter:

  1. "enter," Deut. 23:1, 2 (twice), 3 (twice), 8, 11 (twice), 20, 24, 25
  2. "bring in," Deut. 23:18

Most usages relate to:

  1. people who may not enter (or attend tabernacle events) the congregation of Israel:
    1. damaged males
    2. illegitimate persons or their descendants
    3. Ammonites, Moabites, or their descendants
  2. people who may enter:
    1. Edomites
    2. Egyptians
  3. people who must leave the camp of Israel for a period of time:
    1. males with nocturnal emissions
    2. all Israelites to relieve themselves

▣ "the assembly of the Lord" The phrase "assembly of the Lord" is used of the gathered covenant people of YHWH for worship beginning at Mt. Horeb/Sinai:

  1. Exod. 12:6, "the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel"
  2. Lev. 16:17, "all the assembly of Israel"
  3. Num. 16:3, "all the congregation," "the assembly of the Lord"
  4. Num. 20:4, "the Lord's assembly"
  5. Deut. 5:22, "all your assembly"
  6. Deut. 9:10; 10:4; 18:16, "on the day of assembly"
  7. Deut. 23:1,2,3,8, "assembly of the Lord"
  8. Deut. 31:30, "all the assembly of Israel"
  9. Josh. 8:33, "the people of Israel"

This phrase represents:

  1. worshiping Israel
    1. Mt. Sinai/Horeb
    2. the tabernacle
  2. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 418, based on Jdg. 20:2, asserts that it refers to a leadership council or governing body (cf. Num. 16:3; 20:4)

These excluded ones still have the legal rights of "resident aliens" spelled out in Exod. 22:21; Lev. 19:9-10,33-34; 23:22; Deut. 1:16; 5:14; 27:19.

The Septuagint translated the Hebrew term qahal (BDB 874) as ekklēsia, from which we get the English word, "church." Jesus and the NT authors chose this term to communicate that the New Covenant people of God are to be identified as an extension of the Old Covenant people of God (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-38; Gal. 6:16; 1 Pet. 2:9; Rev. 1:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH (ekklēsia)
